The first pretentious edifice erected in the City of San
Francisco for the special uses of Masonry was begun in
the year 1860, at the corner of Post and Montgomery
streets, the corner stone being laid on Monday, the 25th
day of June-the day following the Anniversary of St.
John Baptist. That building was first occupied by Grand
Lodge at its fourteenth annual communication, commencing Tuesday, the 12th day of May, 1863. It was finished
in 1870, and was imposing to a degree beyond its time.
In his address to Grand Lodge. on the occasion of first
occupying it, Grand Master William C. Belcher said:
"This is the finest and most perfect building upon the
Pacific Coast, and when finished it will be the most
beautiful, if not the most expensive Masonic Temple in
America." It was built during the most trying years
of the civil war, and cost in the neighborhood of $250,000.
The membership in the State in 1863 was six thousand.
The ground space occupied was seventy-five feet on
Montgomery street and one hundred and sixty feet on
(15)

16

DEDICATION OF THE TEMPLE

Post street. To top of balustrade it measured seventy
nine feet, and to top of tower, one hundred and eightynine feet. This splendid building was the Home of
Masons and Masonry continuously until the eighteenth
day of April, 1906, when it was abandoned by order of the
military authorities, and on the .nineteenth of April it
was destroyed by fire.
After some forty years of occupancy, the great
growth of the city and state and the fraternity demanded
that larger and better quarters should be secured, and
on the 12th of October, 1904, Past Grap.cl Maste~ Orrin
S. Henderson introduced a resolution relative to the
disposition ·by the Grand Lodge of its stock in the corpo-:ration owning the Masoni\: Temple, which resolution was
referred to the Finance Committee. On the 14th of October of that year, Past Gdnd Master Oscar Lawler, for
the Finance Committee, reported that the "demand for
the acquisition of quarters sufficiently commod\ous to meet
the requirements is imperative," and further reporting
that a committee of three be appointed to confer and act
with other ·bodies and committees, with the view of
acquiring a site for th,e erection of a new Masonic Temple
in San Francisco. It was also resolved, "that the Grand
Master be empowered to sell all stock of the Masonic Hall
Association owned by Grand Lodge."
At the annual communication of 1905, Brother Reuben
H. Lloyd, chairman of the special committee appointed
to confer with other bodies holding stock in the Temple,
reported, recommending that the old building be razed
and a new and larger structure be erected on the same
site. The matter was rereferred to the same special committee, to report in 1906. Meantime the great fire of
April, 1906, destroyed the building, and Grand Master
Motley H. Flint reported that he had called into consultation as many of the Past Grand Masters and elective
officers as could be secured to talk over the situation,
." and after thorough and exhaustive discussion, it was
decided by more than a majority present that it was for

DEDICATION OF THE TEMPLE

18

In his address to Grand Lodge October 13, 1908,
Grand Master George M. Perine said: "The committee
appointed to select and purchase a site for a new Masonic
Temple in the City of San Francisco, after carefully considering the many pieces of property offered to them ,
unanimously centered upon the property situated on the
west side of Van Ness avenue, between Oak street and
Hickory avenue, having a frontage of 120 feet on Van
Ness · avenue by a uniform depth of 109 feet 9 inches."
Subsequently, in 1909, an additional lot was purchased,
immediately adjoining the original pur.chase, and having
a frontage of 47 feet 9 inches on Oak street by a depth
of 120 feet to Hickory avenue, with an adrlitional frontage
of tl feet on Hickory avenue by a depth of 40 feet. Grand
Lodge approved the report and the purcha,e.
In October, 1908, Brother Benjamin F. Bledsoe introduced the following: "Resolved, that this Grand Lodge
hereby pledges its unstinted aid and influence, and such
financial assistance as its available reso~rces will permit,
to the end that there may be erected on the site selected
a permahent abiding place for the Grand Bodies of this
jurisdiction, adequate to the needs of the craft in our
State and worthy of the name and standing of Masonry in
California." This was referred to the Committee on
Finance, which committee cordially indorsed the sentiments, and Grand Lodge adopted the resolution.
Thus was the preliminary work of the Temple done.
The corner stone was laid October 11 , 1911, and it was
dedicated in ancient form Monday evening, October 13,
1913, the full ceremony thereof following:

And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after

~~~=~l~~:~~ ':or ai~s:~f:r c:rtain standard of n.ational exist:~c~h:n!oc:i~~

~:~s:::n:~s;!~r:f:r~:i~i~:Y :~o:e~~ :~~ea~~~:e t:;:~ll fittingly sym-

bolize their ideal, and use it as a banner or a standard or a coat of
arms, which directs them in all their movements, adorns their public
buiidings, is alluded to by their teachers and orators as a treasure to
be cherished; is loved, admired and respected, nay, even revered, by the
members of its own communities and the citizens and subjects of all
other nations whithersoever dispersed around the globe.
The Israelites unfurled their standard to the world, and their
ideal was "Righteousness," represented, according to tradition, by a
white hand on a blue field, indicating that this, the greatest of ideals"Righteousness"-was within the power of mankind to attain. They
sought no empire, embarked on no wars of conquest, did not design
g.feat commercial ventures, but were insistent and persistent in forcing
upon the world through peaceful means the ideal of "Righteousness."
Rome, whatever other sentiments may be ascribed to her as contributory to the master thought, "Power" seems to have been her ideal, for
law, order, organization and all the other factors were but contributory
to the attainment and wielding of the power of master. To accomplish
this, she necessarily had to prey upon other peoples, fittingly representing this ideal with the eagle, but she, when satiated, died of corruption.
All nations of modern times have their ideals which they emblazon
upon their coat of arms, unfurl to the world and demand respect for it,
just as Israel demanded respect and reverence for her ideal, and Rome
compelled it for herself.
And so we, in common with the rest of the world, have our banner, which is a symbol of our American ideal, a belief that all our citizens here and everywhere enjoy liberty and peace under the protecting
. folds of that banner. They cherish it as the noblest and highest thought
of modern man, and enjoy a sense of security and safety while protected by it. All the world greets our banner with reverence and respect. Under this banner, too, we in the character of Masons may meet
freely and uninterruptedly to conduct all our affairs, and the followers
of a church, or any church, or no church, may bind themselves together
under its folds, for we play no tricky game, we design no treasonable
plots. The game we play is the game of "Equality," and the stakt:s we
play for, "Honor."
We labor for our country, our God and our fellow man, and endeavor to have all our ways directed by righteousness. These are most
fittingly represented by the equal and parallel bars or 5tripes on our
flag, which I now present in the name of Fidelity Lodge No. 120, Free
and Accepted Masons, to the Masonic Temple Association, with the request that it float over this building on all public occasions, and during
all important Masonic gatherings.

At the rondusion of Brother Nieto's remarks, Past
Master Joseph D. Abrams of Fidelity Lodge, cut the cord
which had held the flag from view in the flies of the stage,
and as it gracefully unfolded, the brethren beheld it with
the utmost enthusiasm, and with one accord rose to their
feet and joined with the choir in singing the "Star
Spangled Banner."
Past Grand Master George M. Perine, for the Temple
Association, accepted the banner in the following eloquent
remarks:
M.'. W.'. GRAND MAsTtR, AND BROTHER Nn:ro:

While I am looking at that beautiful flag, Fidelity's gift to the
Masonic Temple Association, I will ask my brethren to do the same.
A more fitting gift could not be selected. Our American Flag to
every American Mason is synonymous of our Masonic Fraternityour flag that the sun never sets on; our fraternal order that the sun
never sets on.
The tournament of the Nations has been swift; that flag first
waved over thirteen states in the wilderness; the American Republic
today has swept from ocean to ocean, it has pushed the light of liberty
to the far ice bounds of Alaska, with a leap it has carried the dawn of
a new day to the Hawaiian Islands and the Philippines; it has exttended
its arms to struggling Cuba and Porto Rico as the champion of Freedom, until today our country. holds the commercial supremacy of the
world, with wealth estimated at more than one trillion dollars, increasing at the rate of over twelve millions a day. That flag floats
over the richest nation of the earth, in men and gold.
I repeat, a more fitting gift could not be given to this Masonic
Fraternity. In the dim past, when our continent was yet untrod by
civilized man, our beloved Institution of Free Masonry lived and
thrived. May we not then draw an inference of the spiritual and
immortal essence of our beloved Masonry from the stability of this
duration-our Institution, of su'ch exceeding antiquity, naturally has seen
many great nations and empires of this earth rise to their zenith and
then fall into oblivion. The great stoics and warriors 0£ that age,
their very names, have been lost to history ; the marble that was
carved with such care to immortalize them has melted away as if they
had been statues of ice.
Despite all this, Masonry has come down to us laden with the
fragrance of its beautiful truths, which unceasingly tell of its undiminished strength and perpetuity-its wisdom, power and might, a

Good fortune and the natural riches of the most fruitful of
God's domain have permitted us to erect here in our home city a
place of worship, which for beauty, purity, simplicity ~nd dignity may
well take its place among the great landmarks of masonry; those
splendid achievements in architecture which have blazed the way from
King Solomon's Temple in the far East to the uttermost confines of
the Wes tern Hemisphere.
As President of the Masonic Temple Association I hereby request
our distinguished Vice-President to deliver into your hands and
possession forever this beautiful building. May we always approach
its portals with a contrite heart and a lowly spirit. Within its walls
may we hold fast to the tenets of our faith; nay more, may ·we
imbibe the great truths of Masonry with a firm determination to
practice them one with the other at home and abroad in every walk
of life.
Finally, when our brothers from distant parts, duly accredited,
knock at our doors, open them gladly; give welcome and see to it
that the fires upon our altar glow with warmth and good cheer, so
that for all time to come, good Masons may find within this Temple a
Hearth and a Home.

David S. Hirshberg to respond on behalf of the stockholders.
MosT WoRSHTPFUL GRAND MASTER AND BRETHRiN oF THE CRAFT:

I join in applauding the eloquent sentiments communicated to us
through Brother Redding, by Brother Crocker, the President of
the Hall Association. On behalf of the stockholders of the Hall
Association I have the great honor to receive this building-this
splendid monument to California genius and Masonic industryand to request the :Most Worshipful Grand Master that it be dedicated by him to the uses and purposes of Masonry.
As we are gathered here tonight in this magnificent temple,
reare'd by the great Masonic fraternity as a memorial to its noble
work, a feeling of sincere regret comes over me, that one who
participated so prominently in the movement for a new Masonic
Temple, is no longer with us. It will be remembered that immediately after the great disaster of 1906, steps were taken under
the leadership of our well beloved Brother Reuben II. Lloyd, for
the consummation of that much-cherished desire on the part of our
great brotherhood. It will be unnecessary to go into details concerning Brother Lloyd's activity, it is suffic:ient to suggest here
to-night, that it was he who selected this ideal location for the
erection of our new Masonic Home. Assodated with Brother Lloyd,

Perhaps no Mason in the jurisdiction of California has ha·d the
·wondedul and successful Masonic experience that Brother Filmer
has had. He has been active in the erection of three stately Masonic
edifices. During the year that he was Worshipful Master of King
Solomon's Lodge No. 260, the magnificent hall and building owned
by that Lodge and its membecs was erected; he participated actively
-very a.ctively-in tbe erection and dedication of the heautiful Scottish Rite Temple, loc.ated at the corner o f Van Ness avenue and
Sutter street, which is a credit to San F rancis.co and a glory to
Masonry; and as before stated, he has peen interested in and connec;ted with this building-the most magnificent of a!I buildings in
this Queen City by the Western sea.
Brother Filmer has been a Mason fifteen years and in that

~paratively short space of time, be has risen to the dignified

position of Grand Master of the large and growing jurisdiction of
California, and in the meantime progressing step by step in closely
relate<l bodies of the craft. He is inspector General of the Scottish
Rite for the Northern Jurisdiction of California; he is f ast Master
of his Lodge ; Past High Priest of his R oyal Arch Chapter; Treasurer of both I.odge and Chapter, and Treasurer of the Western
Addition Masonic Hall Association. I know of no man in the
fraternity whose activities have been so la.rge as his. In view of
all this and his close connection with this building from the very
outset up to this moment, it would seem peculiarly appropriate that
he should be called upon to dedicate th.is hall, the other halls and
rooms herein, and this triumph of architecture, to Masanic uses.
Most Worshipful Grand Master: On behalf of the stockholders,
the brethren of· California, the L odges of California, the Grand Lodge
of California; on behalf of Masonry of California, who, being animated with a desire to .promote the honor and the interest of the
craft, have erected and furnished this building for t heir convenience
and accommodation, I ask you to dedicate the same to Masonic
uses and purposes, agreeably to the ancient forms. and ceremonies
of the Craft.

Yes, my brethren, Masonry is, the champion of orderly, regulated government, the defender of freedom, and teaches that no
state, no nation can be great, or its people prosperous and happy
without just and. equal laws, equally and justly administered.
Masonry is the patron of the sciences and the arts-of the
sciences which have reared the beneficent structure of civilizationof the arts which have 1beautified it. She recognizes that this
beautiful structure of civilization, from turret to foundation-stone,
is the result of labor of hand and brain, and labor she exalts.
Labor in the quarry, procuring the Rough Ashlar, and in the workshop preparing the Perfect Ashlar; labor in the studio of Phidias
fashioning into classic beauty lifeless marble and breathing into it
the soul of a goddess; labor of the poet singing to us of Paradise,
of the historian garnering the lessons of ages dead and gone ;
labor at the easel of Rubens moving the heart to unutterable emotion by the "Descent from the Cross" or of a Turner transferring
to canvas the dappled morning, the tranquil beauty of the purple
hills, the fading glory of retreating day; labor of the composer,
making the air to vibrate with celestial harmony and ravishing
our hearts with sublime and heavenly symphonies; lahor in the
pulpit expounding the Holy Bible and "justifying the ways of God
to man" ; labor of the scientist, wresting from nature her most
hidden secrets and conquering the malignant enemies that prey on
life; labor on Mount Hamilton, measuring, weighing the stars as
they speed onward, and tracing the mysterious path of the comet
as it pursues its flight, "lone, wandering, but not lost" ; labor of
the lawgiver, laying broad and deep the foundation of wise and
stable government and formulating laws for the safe-guarding of
life and liberty; labor on the bench, patient and merciful, administering God's justice on earth; labor in the deep, dark mine that
mankind may be lighted and warmed and industry rewards the
countless hands of toil ; labor on the earth ploughing, planting,
reaping the prairies, tunneling the mountains, felling . the forests,
erecting habitations, guiding the lightning, conquering the air ; labor
on the sea-carrying the products of industry from land to land
and bringing into harmonious relation once alien and hostile peoples
-manly, godlike labor, thou hast nobly performed thy appointed
task and behold the work of thy hands. Law, order, government;
literature, science, art; the earth made habitable, human life prolonged, and mankind, risen from ignorance to knowledge, from
bondage to freedom, approaching nearer and nearer, day by day,
to that long dreamed-of hour when Justice shall be <;_rowned and
from her throne of beauty rule the world !

DEDICATION OF THE TEMPLE
DEDICATION OF THE TEMPLE

And it is beeat1·se Masonry exafts labor that we treas\lre the
memory of the Operative Masons te> whom we are indebted for
whatever makes our Order symmetrical and enduring, wQrthy and
beneficent. They builded better than they knew. We see them toiling through the centuries; we see them exemplifying the beauties of
harmony, the blessing of union, the virtue of obedience, and the
necessity for law; we see the useful and reverent work of their
master hands-the palace, the temple, the cathedral rising in majestic
beauty and exciting the wonder and admiration of alt time; we
see them laying the foundation of a spiritual temple-the temple
of Free and Accepted Masonry, which shall exist as long as love
stands by a human grave, as long as man has faith in God, practices Charity, worships Justice and yearns for immortality.
Yes, my brethren, we may well pay grateful tribute to the
Operative Masons. "If they were unacquainted with the works. of
phtlosophers and poets, they were deeply read in the oracles. of God.
If their names were not found in the registers of heralds, they
were recorded in the Book of 'Life." Rest, rest in thy unmarked
grave, 0 humble Mason. The temple we are dedicating tonight
is the fruit of thy labor, a monument to thy memory. As. long as
gratitude abides in Masonic hea·rts thy name, thy glory shall not die.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, two years ago we laid the corner-stone of this temple. Our faith has been justified, our hope
realized. I would renew and prolong the prayer I then was privileged to utter.
May this temple be a- home of nourishment for the poor, the
weary and heavy-laden. May it be a place of joy for eyes dimmed
by tears, for hearts bowed down by grief, for the distressed in body
and in mind. May the gladsome light of morning play upon its
walls; may the lingering rays of the evening reflect its' glory. May
it stand for generations yet to be, immune from fire and shock,
welcoming to its fraternal hospitality the Masons of California and
of all lands.
But, oh, if it should fall, like that other beloved temple, if it
should be consumed by fire or overwhelmed by disaster, the principles and truths for which it stands will not perish in its ruins.
Those principles are immutable, those truths are immortal, and being
of celestial origin they cannot die, they will survive the wreck of matter and the crash of worlds.. Oh, may this temple stand, watched over
and guarded by the approving stars of heaven, and when it falls, if
fall it must, may our brothers yet unborn erect another and even
more glorio~ and worthy temple to Masonry and to God.

Committee on Credentials requested further time in which

Prior to opening Grand Lodge, Past Grand Master
William T. Lucas asked permission to speak, which was
granted, and he said:
MosT WORSHIPFUL GRAND MAs'l'JtR: Since. the great fire of 1906
this Grand Lodge has been without the furniture necessary for the
proper conduct of a Lodge, and at its Annual Communications has
depended upon the generosity of the Lodges of San Francisco for
gavels, columns and altar furniture, with the single exception .of
one gavel presented by Past Grand Master Oscar Lawler, which
gavel was fashioned from wood taken out of the old battleship Constitution-Old Ironsides. It is now my pleasure, in behalf of our
Grand Secretary, to present to you, for the use of the Grand Wardens, two silver-mounted gavels made from wood out of the oldest
battleship in the American navy-the Independence.
The history of Freemasonry appeals to those who believe in the
aphorism "That free hands with fettered - thought · is the basest · of
all· slavery."
The men who organized our independence and perfected our
Charter of American freedom were members of our Grand Order.
Those who have been true to the highest ideals of American citizenship have been members of our Craft.

53

The glorious history enacted by our navy is emblazoned on
every page of our country's greatness. ·

,

Old Ironsides and the Independence are synonyms of endurance
and American bravery.
The Independence was built in 1812-under the special supervision of Commodore Bainbridge-the War Dog of the American
Navy. In 1815 she joined the Mediterranean squadron of Stephen
Decatur, the greatest naval officer that ever trod the deck of a
man-of-war's man, and was a component part of the first great fleet
that our country ever sent to foreign waters. Her seventy-four
guns had much to do with blockading the Algerian ports and the
subjugation of the Barbary States.
'
The Independence first appeared on the Pacific Coast in 1848
as the flagship of Commodore Shubrick, and in her thre~ years of
service on the Hesperian shores of our great Republic participated
in the capture of Guaymas and Mazatlan. .In 1851 she returned to
the Atlantic coast and a little later served as flagship in the Mediterranean.
When Mare Island Navy Yard was established in 1854, the
Independence was sent to New York, refitted, , and sailed to San
Francisco to become a guardship, being anchored ·off Third Street.
In 1856 the last chapter in the history of this the oldest man-of-war's
man in the American Navy was begun, when she was transferred
to Mare Island to be used for testing the sectional floating drydocks.
In 1858 she was made a receiving ship, and now rides in the mud
near where she was anchored fifty-five years ago.
.
She is a. memory-but her wood is harder than anything save
iron. Her history reflects credit on her officers and men : American valor and patriotism. Her naval activity and brainy commanders
~id ~uch to conserve the ~eace of the world ; albeit ready to fight
m a JUSt cause when required.
·
Her history spells faith, fullness and devotion to duty, and
should be an inspiration to every Mason. As this old vessel
touched closely the life of our Nation, so does Masonry touch our
national life, but only for peace-Universal Peace.
These gavels I now present to the Grand Wardens, knowing
~ull well that they will always be cherished, and used only in the
interest of the best manhood and the best citizenship.

Brother Benjamin F. Bledsoe, Grand Senior Warden,
responded most eloquently a~d. accepted the gift for the
Grand Lodge.

PRAYER.
Supreme Grand Architect of the Universe! Grateful to Thee
for all the countless blessings and mercies we have received at Thy
hands, we assemble for the sixty-fourth Annual Communication of
this Grand Lodge to worship Thee, and transact the business to
come before it, to Thy honor and the benefit of our brethren of the
mystic tie. And 0 our Father, bless Thou the work of our hands,
lead us in love by Thy good counsel here, and when our labors
on earth are finished, receive us into Thine own house "not made
with hands, eternal in the heavens." Amen.

ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge,
F. & A . M. of Califo,.ia:
With reverence and gratitude to the Great Architect of the Universe we meet here today in this magnificent Temple, only last night
dedic~ted to the Grand and beneficent purposes of Masonry, symbolic
of the enduring strength and beauty of our Order, and I am pleased
to welcome to the sixty-fourth Annual Communication of our Grand
Lodge the representatives of over fifty thousand Masons whose names
are borne upon the roster of three hundred and fifty-five Lodges.
Well may we congratulate ourselves that after seven years we
are again happily domiciled amid such splendid surroundings; environments which, in their beautiful appointments and embellishments,
breathe the very spirit of our great Institution.
While this grand and stately Temple has, in great measure, been
erected by brethren comparatively young in Masonic work, it is
fitting that we should remember with grateful hearts those whose

55

NECROLOGY.

While we are •complacently enjoying the present moment, let
us pause, in loving remembrance, to pay homage to those who have
fallen in our midst during the past year, for three beloved members
of this Grand Lodge have passed to the great beyond.
On the evening of Friday, November 29th, 1912, our Brother
Henry Sayre Orme, Past Grand Master, was called to the eternal
temple of rest, and no more among men will be seen his genial and
pleasant smile; no more will the influence of his beautiful character
be felt except as the wafting perfume of a fragrant flower. Born
in Georgia in 1837, he came to California in his early manhood and
grew with the great State of his adoption. His zeal, energy and
splendid talents brought to him the highest honors in Masonry.
Brother Orme served the Grand Lodge as Grand Master in 1894
and most ably discharged the duties of his high ~ffice. He exempli~
fied to an unusual degree the lessons of charity, and permitted not
even the practice of his chosen profession, that of medicine, to interfere with what he considered his Masonic duty. His funeral
services were conducted under the auspices of the Grand Lodge of
California by M.". w:. Dana R. Weller, Past Grand Master.
The next to pass to the great beyond was Brother William Schuyler Moses, our Grand Bible Bearer, who quietly and painlessly departed this life on the ninth day of December, 1912. Having been
made a Mason in the State of New York in 1849, he reached the
land where he was destined to spend the years of his manhood in
time to be present at the organization of our Grand Lodge, April
19, 1850, in the City of Sacramento. With his demise, so far as we
know, passes the last of those who had actual and personal knowledge of the events of those very early days of our Fraternity in
California. Tall, majestic, dignified, and patriarchal, Brother Moses
was a striking figure in our assemb~ies. The sweetness of his personality, his animated conversations, full of anecdote and reminiscence, will long be remembered by the fraternity of our great State.
On Saturday, the twelfth day of April, 1913, while visiting San
Buenaventura Lodge No. 214, at Ventura, l was inexpressibly shocked
upon the receipt of a telegram from Brother Whicher, our Grand
Secretary, advising me of the sudden death of our beloved Grand

li6

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Treasurer, Brother Edward Coleman. .His long, useful and eminently successful life was brought to a close at his home in San
Francisco on that morning. Brother Coleman was a native of Walton, England, but came to America while quite a young man. He
crossed the plains to California with his brother, John C. Coleman,
in 1853, and engaged in mining in Grass Valley, where both brothers
received the light of Masonry in Madison Lodge No. 23. Brother
Coleman often remarked that his early manhood was beneficently
influenced by the beautiful teachings of our Order, and he was
wont frequently to attribute his splendid succe~ to his early absorption of the precepts and principles of Masonry. His great business acumen, his accurate judgment, supplemented by an integrity
as firm as adamant, enabled him to amass the fortune which he
later devoted to high philanthropic purposes. His able handling of
the funds of our Grand Lodge, his great assistance as a director
of the Masonic Temple' Association; his unerring judgment in our
councils of deliberation, caused him to be invaluable to our Grand
Lodge. The beautiful hospital which he erected, equipped a~d presented to the Masonic Home at Decoto; his generous bequest in his
will to our Masonic Homes, are substantial testimonials of his love
and reverence for our great Institution.
Upon the death of Brother Moses, I appointed w.·. Brother
Samuel E. Burke as Grand Bible· Bearer, 'and w:. Brother John
C. Coleman, brother of our late Grand Trea~urer, to succeed Edward
Coleman in that important Office.

VISITATIONS AND PUBLIC CJ!RJ!MONIALS.

Being firmly impressed with the general good which results to
the craft from the official visits of the Grand Master and believing
also that a knowledge of conditions of the several Lodges can only
be properly obtained from personal observation, I endeavored to
make these visits as extensive and as far reaching as my time would
permit.
Our great State covers an immense area and because of the
large number of Lodges and the geographical immensity of the jurisdiction, it is a physical impossibility to visit all, and therefore I aimed
to include as many as possible by holding district meetings; several
Lodges from different localities often being represented on the same
evening. By this plan some sixty-one Masonic districts, representing
over three hundred Lodges, were visited, and I believe much good
resulted from the increased interest manifested by such occasions.
I was frequently accompanied on these trips by our Grand Lecturer, Brother Thomas ]. Baker, who rendered invaluable assistance,
not only by outlining itineraries for visitations, but also through his
intimate knowledge of the individual conditions surrounding the
Lodges and districts. It is impossible to realize the great value of
this most competent and indefatigable officer of our Grand Lodge,
unless one is close at hand when he is visiting the Lodges and imparting instruction to the brethren. I take this opportunity to express my personal gratitude to him for his numerous acts of courtesy and unselfish kindness.
During these visitations I was privileged to have the honor of
raising thirty brethren to the sublime degree of Master Mason ; of
constituting ten new Lodges ; of installing the officers of twentythree subordinate Lodges ; of laying the cornerstone of three Masonic
Temples and four public buildings, and of dedicating · three Masonic
Temples to the purposes of Masonry.
My first official visit was made October 24th, 1912, to that old •
historic Lodge, California No. 1, where, at the invitation of the Worshipful Master, Harvey A. Marvin, I conferred the third degree of
Masonry upon William B. Faville, the Architect of the new Masonic
Temple at San Francisco.
On October 30th, I was privileged to visit Starr King Lodge No.
344 and conferred the third degree in that Lodge.
The next visit was made to Sequoia Lodge No. 349, on November
2, the occasion being the celebration of its tenth anniversary. The
ladies were present, as also was M.'. w:. William S. Wells, Past
Grand Master, who was Grand Master when the dispensation to
labor was granted to this Lodge.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

On November 19, 1912, I visited Bakersfield Lodge No. 224, and
at the request of the Worshipful Master again conferred the third
degree. A most enjoyable evening followed.
November 21, 1912, I convened Grand Lodge at El Centro, in
Imperial County, and in the afternoon laid the cornerstone of the
Masonic Temple of El Centro Lodge No. 348; and in the evening
of the same day, convening in. the Lodge room of El Centro Lodge,
constituted Holtville Lodge No. 425. The following evening, in the
town of Brawley, it was my pleasure to enjoy the unusual honor of
conferring the sublime degree of Master Mason upon twin brothers.
The brethren of Imperial County are especially worthy of commendation in their splendid Masonic work, as it is but little more than
nine years since the first house was erected in this wonderfully fertile section of our great State. The brethren have builded well.
Earnest Masonic enthusiasm prevails, and the Lodges at El Centro,
Imperial, Calexico, Brawley and Holtville are playing a deserving
part in the moral upbuilding of this new and progressive community.
On the evening of November 30th, I visited the Lodge of the
twenty-seventh Masonic District, the meeting being held in the Masonic Temple at Stockton. The Inspectors of the Bay Counties and
the Grand Lecturer accompanied me, and the third degree was conferred by the Grand Master, assisted by the Inspectors. On this
occasion the lecture was delivered to three brothers, two of whom
were invested with the degree in the afternoon of the same day.
This meeting was largely attended.
A reception was tendered the Grand Master by his own Lodge,
King Solomon's No. 260, at San Francisco, on the evening of December 2, 1912.
The loyalty and generous spirit of the brethren of the several
Lodges at San Francisco was beautifully expressed by an exceedingly
large and enthusiastic reception to the Grand Master on the evening
of December 7th in the Scottish Rite Hall. Several thousand Masons
• and their families were present on this delightful occasion, and the
Grand Master was deeply touched by the warm fraternal greeting
of his brethren of his own home City and their evident pleasure at
his elevation to the highest honor in the gift of the brethren of the
State.
An official visit was made to Eden Lodge No. 113, December
14, at San Leandro, and a profitable and enjoyable evening experienced. The Grand Master on this occasion presented the candidate
with an apron which had been presented to the initiate's father some
forty years before by the same Lodge.
On the evening of December 16th 1 was accorded the honor,
by the gracious courtesy of the Worshipful Master, Brother Herman

Grand Lodge was conveneq :by me at Santa Barbara and the
~~~nerstone of the Government postoffice building w;is laid June
27th. ·A reception to the Grand Master was tendered in ·the evening
by· i:?anta Barbara Lodge No. 192 and Magnolia Lodge No. 242.
Fairmount Lodge U. D., at San Francisco, was visited June
24th, the Grand Master conferring the third degree. This Lodge,
working but a few months under dispensation, manifests a splendid
spirit arid is doing true Masonic work. .
'
Imbued with the . thought that our generous brethren . of the
Hawaiian Islands deserved every consideration possible for our Grand
Lodge to extend to them, I left San Francisco with our Grand Lecturer, Brother Baker, and Brother H. G. Ilderton of Oak Grove
Lodge No. 115, on July 2d, arriving at Honolulu July 8th. The
warm and balmy climate of our beautiful Island possessions seems
to be transmitted to the fervent fraternal hearts of our Masonic
brethren in this delightful part of our jurisdiction. We visited
Kilauea Lodge No. 330 at Hilo, on the Island of Hawaii, on the
evening of July 10th, and found abundant evidence of Masonic
zeal and enthusiasm. The brethren there have erected one of the
finest Masonic Temples of the entire jurisdiction. On Monday evening
of July 14th, at the Masonic Temple of Honolulu, a reception was
tendered the Grand Master and the brethren above mentioned, by
Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, Oceanic No. 371 and Honolulu No. 400,
and the following evening a sumptuous dinner was enjoyed at the
Country Club with the Past Masters and Officers of those three
Lodges.
Durant Lodge No. 268 was visited on the evening of A1,1gust
7th, the Grand Master conferring the. degree of Master Mason.
From August 18th to the 30th some of the beauties and grandeur
of the great timber and agricultural portions of our State were enjoyed in company with Brother. Baker and M.". w:. George M.
Perine, Past Grand Master.
Visitations were made to the Lodges at Fort Bragg, Willits,
Eureka, Crescent City, Yreka, Dunsmuir, Redding, Willows and Arbuckle. District meetings were held at all of these towns.
On the evening of September 1st the Grand Master was accorded
the pleasure of conferring the third degree upon a candidate in the
new Masonic Temple at San Francisco. This was the first Masonic
degree conferred in the Temple, and the Grand Master was accorded
this privilege through the generous courtesy of Hermann Lodge
No. 127.
Visits were also made to California Lodge No. 1 on September
4th, and to Mission Lodge No. 169 on September 6th.

A visit was ma?e Monday evening, September 22d, to Plumas·

at Oroville. Large and .enthusiastic . meetings were held at each of
these places, and entertainment was kindly arranged for the G d

It is the duty of the Inspe~or to report the condition of the
Lo~s of his district on the !st day of September of each year. I
suggest that such date be changed to July . 1st for the reason that
the Grand Master is more busily engaged during the . months of
September and October than at any other time of ii1~· year, and
can not give proper attention to the many suggestions contained in
the Inspectors' reports.
I also desire at this time to extend my sincere thanks to all
the brethren of our jurisdiction with whom I have come in contact during my term of office, individually and collectively. Wherever I have traveled throughout our great jurisdiction, from its
northern to its southern boundary, from its mountain sides to the
Pacific Ocean and the islands of the sea, I was received with such
eviden~ of kindness as rendered every duty a pleasure.
Especially, however, do I acknowledge a debt of gratitude to our
most efficient Grand Secretary, Brother Whicher, whose invaluable
advice and assistance have been freely and generously given. And
to Brother Harry Johnson for many courtesies, and also to Brothers
Angellotti, and Patton, whose able assistance has also been unselfishly
extended to me.

MASONIC HOMJ!S.

I am pleased to report that, through the indefatigable efforts
of the Trustees, the Home at Decoto is now in better condition than ever
before. Last year the Trustees reported: "We have suffered with
others from the dry season, and practically from the first of June
we have been without water in our reservoirs. All toilets, bathtubs, wash basins, faucets, except in the kitchen have been shut off
and it has been necessary to haul wate~ for all'household puri)oses:•;
Another dry year accentuated this deplorable condition, and. this
Home faced a most serious state of affairs, that of a water famine.
• The expected development of the springs had failed; the test l>Orinrs
on the fiat near the barns produced no results, and it was."again
necessary to resort to hauling water a considerable distance. · The
buildings were again without protection from fire and the · i~ates
were necessarily required to use water in scant quantity, and "'t he
flowers, shrubbery and garden suffered accordingly. But· 'without
losing faith, the Trustees actively continued the search for ~at~r
and in February their efforts were splendidly rewarded with an abun~
dant supply, secured by boring on the lower fiat near the county
road. A pumping test was made and one hnndred and ninety gallons of water per minute was pumped without any diminntion .in
quantity. This most · satisfactory result encouraged the Board .. to
install a pumping plant affording adequate faciljtics,, not only · for
present, but for future need$. All this necessitated aJJ expense .of
some $3000.00 more than the appropriation of $5CXX>.OO. yoted by tJic
Grand Lodge at its last Annual Communication, . an"d" this expense
I approved in conformity with the resolution passed at that · session.
There is now an abundance of that most necessary element of our
daily needs which, flowing so copiously after two or three ·dry · seasons, insures e'vcn· increased supply ·in -the years to come-.
Owing to the present crowded condi.tion of the quarters of · the
inmates and the necessity of providing additional rooms for the
constantly increasing number of applicants, the Grand Lodge, at ·its
last Annual Communication, levied an additional tax on the subordinate
Lodges for the purpose of erecting permanent buildi11gs, and ' not-

Accepte~

A few weeks later, in response to a circular letter from the
Grand Secretary of Illinois, calling for assistance, $1000.00 was dispatched to the Grand Master of that jurisdiction for the sufferers
in that State.
Assistance was also tendered to our brethren in the flood districts of Indiana, but the Grand Master of that jurisdiction responded
that happily they were able to care for all their distresses without
outside aid.
Our brethren of Ohio and · Illinois gave ample and abundant
evidence of their gratitude by fervent and thankful letters from
their Grand Masters.
It is proper to state here that the most generous subscriptions
for this relief were made by our zealous and warm hearted brethren
of the Hawaiian Islands. Hawaiian Lodge No. 21 cabled $1000.00;
Honolulu Lodge No. 409, $250.00, and Oceanic Lodge No. 371, $200.00;
all of these contributions being received by the Grand Master before
his letters, calling upon our brethren for assistance, reached the

·. GntMANIA LODGI!.

A Petition has been received from a number of brethren in the
City of Los Angeles to organize a Lodge in that city to be called
Germania Lodge. . The petition requested that the dispensation be
granted to work in the German language. Construing the intent of
our Constitution in regard to the organization of new Lodges to
refer to Lodges working in the English language only, I refused to
grant a dispensation to work in the German language, but I issued
a dispensation to work in English, and their petition for a charter
will be presented at this communication. I see no objection to this
Grand Lodge granting a dispensation or charter to work in the
German language if it is deemed expedient to do so.
An application has been received from Burlingame Lodge No.
400, in accordance and in compliance with section 92a of the Constitution, requesting the Grand Lodge to pass a resolution enlarging
its jurisdiction to include a part of the corporate limits of the town
of San Mateo. At the present time each of these Lodges has exclusive jurisdiction over the corporate limits of their respectivie
towns, and the Grand Master deems it inadvisable to make any
change which would cause one Lodge to encroach upon and include
part of the _c orporate limits of another town, and refuses to recommepd the passage of such a re~olution by this Grand Lodge.
CLANDl!STINt .AND FAKt MASONRY.

While irregular and clandestine bodies of so called Masons still
continue to organize and make fitful endeavors to keep alive, such
bodies do no harm to our Craft in general except that, in order to
maintain their existence, dissolute characters are admitted to their
ranks who parade the square and compass, much to the disgust of
regular Masons. Such persons often fleece the unwary, either by
inducing them to pay a fee for their fake goods, or by a talc of
distress accompanied with a request for relief.
In October of last year an organizer for the "American Federation of Masons" named Kay was arrested in Oakland and charged
with obtaining money under false .pretenses. One Wm. C. Cavitt,
styled "Grand Master of the American Federation of Masons for
the District Grand Lodge of California," defended Kay in the Police

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

74

Court and stayed proceedings until February, 1913, when it was
tried by a jury which disagreed. The case was retried again in
April by a jury, which found the defendant guilty, and the Court
sentenced him to jail for six months. Cavitt appealed the case, and
we are informed that the Superior Court affirmed the sentence of
the lower court.
In July, 1913, a young man pretending to be deaf and dumb was
arrested by police officers in San Francisco, charged with begging
on the streets by handing out to passers-by slips of paper stating
thereon that he was a Mason and a member of Livingston Lodge
No. 32, Montana. Officers took the culprit to the office of Grand
Secretary, where he soon began to talk. A complaint was lodged
against . him for illegally wearing the insignia of a Mason (he wore
a pin having square and compasses in the buttonhole of his coat),
and on conviction in Police Court was given six months in the county
jail. Name of imposter was given as Frank Marion. It was shown
that he had served three terms in the penitentiary.
One of the most notorious and persistent Masonic frauds who
ever operated in America is George E. Holt, who has renounced his
clandestine work and publicly confessed his sins. The following from
the ''Trestle Board," a Masonic publication of San Francisco of date
March, 1913, fully explains the history of his operations here and
the punishment meted out to him :
The Trestle Board, in its February number, reported the conviction of George E. Holt, degree peddler, who has been operating in
San Francisco for the past five years (with. the exception · of one
year, which he served in a Massachusetts jail) of obtaining money
under false pretenses. The prosecuting witness in the case was
Howard E. Murray, upon whom Holt had, for a consideration of $20,
conferred the title of "Right Worshipful," and to whom he represented that the "degrees" which he conferred entitled the recipient to
the privilege of visiting in "any" Lodge of A. F. & A. M. outside , the
State of California." The prisoner pleaded guilty and offered a prayer
for prpbation, confessing his fraudulent practices, acknowledging that
he is not a member of any regularly constituted Lodge of Masons,
and that he is not authorized to confer Masonic degrees, and prom- '
ising if given a chance to support his wife and children, to never '
engage in any business pertaining to Masonry. He furthermore delivered all his printed matter and paraphernalia to the Court for destruction.

DtCISIONS.

During the past year the correspondence of the Grand Master ·
has been voluminous and many hours each day have been consumed
by a stenographer and typist, notwithstanding the fact that much
of the work has been handled by the Grand Secretary's office.
Questions of policy and of interpretation . of Masonic law a~e
of almost daily occurrence and it is to the credit of our Masomc
brethren that very few inquiries have been of a frivolous nature;
indeed in nearly all instances the questions asked indicate an earnest
desire' on the part of the brethren to conform to the Constitution in
every particular.
Although many rulings have been made during the year, there
are but seven that I deem of sufficient importance to report. They
are as follows:
t. The question was asked whether it is . a violation of ?ur
. Masonic law to print the names of candidates on postal card notices
sent to Lodge members informing them of the time of special meeting for the conferring of the degree.
Under section 77L of the Constitution it is unlawful to pu?lis~
the names of applicants for degrees in a printed folder, and if tt
is a violation of our law to publish names of candidates for the
degrees in a printed folder, it is also wrong to print them ?n postal
cards, and I ruled against the printing of names of candidates or
applicants on postal card notices, folders or cards.
2. The fee of an applicant does not become a part of the reve~ue
of the Lodge until the applicant is elected by the Lodge to rece1v.e
the degrees. From the time the fee is received by the Lodge until
such time as the applicant is elected or rejected the Lodge holds
such fee in trust and in case of rejection must stand ready to return
the fee to the applicant, and that in computing the ten per cent "for

77

purposes of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse"
the fees of rejected applicants should be deducted.
3. A Lodge has the right to collect additional dues from a
brother who paid his dues in advance for a year and received a
receipt for dues to December 31st, the Lodge on May 1st having
increased the dues from six dollars to nine dollars per annum.
"The brother, although in possession of a receipt for dues for
a full year, should pay the increase from the time such increase of
dues took effect in the Lodge. The increase affected all the brethren
and although the Lodge, in good faith, issued a receipt for dues
for a year for the amount then in force, and the Lodge, during
that year, increased the dues of its members, the brother should pay
the increase just the same as other brethren who did not pay in
advance.
4. "The son of a Master Mason, after he has passed the age
of majority, or the sister or mother of a Master Mason is not entitled
as a matter of right, to Masonic charity, but certain conditions may
prevail where such son, sister or mother, being helpless and incompetent to sustain themselves, and dependent upon the brother for
support, and the brother being unable to extend relief to them, the
Lodge may, by extending relief to the son, sister or mother, relieve
the brother himself.
5. Question-An Entered Apprentice Mason from a foreign Lodge
presents a dimit and asks to be elected and advanced.
What procedure is to be followed and is any consent from the
Foreign Lodge necessary?
"If the paper possessed by the E. A emanates from a Lodge
under the jurisdiction of any Grand Body recognized as legitimate
by this Grand Lodge, and is in the form of a dimit, it may be
accepted as the official consent of such Lodge to the advancement
of the E. A. by any other Lodge ( sec. 113 Const.) and the waiver
of jurisdiction of such Lodge referred to in the last paragraph of
sec. 155, Const. and no other official consent from the Foreign Lodge
is necessary to enable your Lodge to receive his application for the
remaining degrees.
"The procedure to be followed in such a case is declared by the
last paragraph of section 155, Const. and of course includes payment
of fees, reference of application to a committee, report of committee
and election by the Lodge.
"Before receiving the application, the Master should of course
satisfy himself that the applicant is the person referred to in the
so-called dimit, and that he has in fact received the degree indicated
therein."

In the year 1881 the me

1903 t h e 25 •000

membership has reached the grand total of over 50,000 Master Masons,
the Order having gained, in the last ten years, as many members as
it recorded after the first fifty-three years of its existence. This
rapid increase, however, I believe has been consistent and in harmony with the splendid growth of our State and does not in any
manner indicate that our Lodges are not exercising proper care
in the consideration of applicants for membership therein.
Occasionally, of course, we unfortunately find men in our midst,
as evidenced by the trials now and then conducted by our subordinate
Lodges, who flagrantly violate and persist in violating their Masonic
obligations. Such men should be disciplined, and neither the favor
of friends nor the charity of the Lodge should operate to prevent
a proper punishment for their delinquencies.
I touch upon this matter because too frequently in Lodge trials
the friends of accused members, honestly believing that leniency and
charity should be extended to the erring brother, lend their aid to
defeat the e~ds of justice. As Masons, we espouse the highest moral
principles and it is incumbent upon us to manifest to the outside world .
our absolute disapproval ·of the criminal and immoral who may exist
among our membership. There is no condonation of crime in Masonry.
From personal observation and knowledge I am highly pleased to
report an excellent condition of our Order throughout the State.
In the larger centers great interest is manifested and enlivened, not
only by the ever increasing degree work, but by many of the Lodges
providing profitable and instructive entertainment for their own members and the visiting brethren. Interchange of visitations among the
Lodges; lectures on Masonic and kindred subjects by those competent to deliver them; travelogues assisted by stereoscope and moving pictures; occasional banquets with their attendant instructive
speeches, largely assist in maintaining the interest of the brethren
in our Order. The members of California Lodge No. 1 have presented with splendid histrionic ability an interesting play of an
"Eighteenth Century Lodge," Masonic in its nature and highly entertaining and instructive. Such diversion from the ordinary ritualistic
work is productive of inestimable good, and Masters of Lodges and
Inspectors of Districts should, whenever possible, provide and encourage such form of instructive diversion.
But while the Craft is generally prosperous and the Lodges making a healthy growth, there are a few not so fortunate: Some of our
older mining towns, once large in population and teeming with wealth
and affluence, are now mere shadows of what they formerly were.
The young men have sought the larger centers, leaving few behind
except the ag.ed, and the Lodges in such · towns are hardly maintaining an existence.

80

PROCEEDINGS OF 'l'HE

Reports from the Inspectors of sixty-six districts are replete
with suggestion and advice, and indicate the splendid work of these
officers. From their reports we learn of the condition of Lodges
comprising the several districts; we learn of those Lodges which conform faithfully to the laws and regulations, and of those that are
lax and slipshod in their work. The latter, however, we are pleased
to report, are exceedingly few.
The Secretaries and Treasurers of some of our Lodges do not
present semi-annual reports, and many of the Lodges have not adopted
the card index system for visitors recommended by M.". w:. Brother.
Monroe at the last Communication of the Grand Lodge. These are
important matters that the Masters of our Lodges may well see to
in their respective Lodges.
Some of our Inspectors suggest an increased amount for the
minimum dues, claiming that six dollars annually are insufficient
to defray the expenses of many of the Lodges whose dues are but
six dollars a year. I am inclined to agree in this suggestion, and
believe that our. Lodges would be in better financial condition were
the minimum dues nine dollar! per annum . .
CONCLUSION.

The present year of Masonry is very near its close and well may
we felicitate ourselves that it has been one of general prosperity
to our beloved Order; that no great calamity, local or otherwise,
has disturbed or retarded the happiness of the people of our great
State.
The wheels of industry have been rapidly turning; agricultural
development has been unequaled; from the bowels of the earth have
come forth its mineral wealth in lavish abundance ; from its giant
trees have been taken a mighty harvest of timber; science has harnessed its mountain streams to pour forth its liquid power and light
to· every City and hamlet; peace, prosperity and apparent contentment
have been the lot of all. In a clime so gentle and a State so lavish
in its natural gifts, the growth of intellectual and moral development
is keeping pace with its material growth. Earnest, honest men and
women everywhere are zealously striving for higher things. Societies
and organizations are laboring for the suppression of vice in all its
hideous forms. Men of intellect and high moral worth are wrestling
with the social problems of the time; legislatures and police courts
are enacting laws whose objects are to enforce public morality. But
the well informed recognize the fact that reform must come from
within and if we would rise to nobler levels the high ideals of Masonry
must be put into full activity in the ordinary and common affairs of
life.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

81

The influence of one man whose life is guided by the hallowed
light of Masonry, is far beyond estimation.
One may build a mansion; may expend uncounted sums in rearing its walls of marble, and in storing it with every element of beauty
within; and yet, passing from this mortal realm, may have accomplished but little; while another, perhaps, never built anything save
the beautiful mansion of character. The invisible precious stones
t~at are laid in the walls of the new Temple, he laid around about
his own character. He left little save influence, but that influence,
e:certed day by day, falls into sensitive souls, and shapes, moulds and
directs the course of life, and reveals the truth to countless others.
Thus, my brethren, must the beneficent work of Masonry go
f~rward, patient in its strength for ideal humanity, adding link upon
lmk to the chain which joins the man of the past, through the man
of the present, to the better man of the future.
WILLIAM P. FILMER,
Grand Master.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lrxlge of California:
I present herewith my annual report, which has been prepe.red dur·
ing a time of unusual labor: for what with preparing for the dedication of the new Temple, the closing of the work of indexing the names
of members of the jurisdiction, the removal of the office from the
old quarters, and the ordinary work of collecting the annual returns
of Lodges and the new tax for a building fund for the Masonic Homes, ·
the summer and fall days have been strenuous ones.
By order of the Grand Master, the office of the Grand Secretary
was on the 27th day of September removed to the Masonic Temple.
The offices comprise rooms for the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary,

•
86

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the Grand Lecturer, a general reading room for Masons (which room
is fitted up with cases holding some fifteen hundred books, at this time
principally reports of other jurisdictions), a "stack room" for books,
and a store room. Twenty-four large boxes of books containing the
Pierce Library, have been opened and the contents placed upon
shelves. The matter of cataloging will necessarily take some umc.
and will not be undertaken until after Grand Lodge. Meantime, however, the rooms are furnished for the comfort and convenience of the
brethren, and it is hoped many will avail themselves of the hospitalitj
thereof.

The unfinished business for consideration at this communication is
the resolution of Brother Henry M. Owens, as follows :

The matter of indexing the name and Masonic history of each
member in the jurisdiction has progressed in a fairly satisfactory way.
I have entered and filed in alphabetical order every name and history
as returned by the several Secretaries. Generally, those officers were
prompt and careful in making returns for the index, but one hundred
and six Lodges, the names of whose members, as shown by the last
Roster, had been mailed to Secretaries in August and September, 1912,
had not reported up to the 4th of April, 1913, at which date they were
again requested to respond; again on the 22d of May they were written to, and before the 1st of August. all had sent in corrected name~
and histories except twenty-one Lodges. I therefore caused to be
made up in this office, from the records of 1906 and the years following to 1912, an index of the names and Masonic histories of the members of those missing Lodges-not a satisfactory list, but the best I
could do. The work of indexing and correcting the spelling of names
on the roll, as reported by Secretaries, resulted in the changing of the
spelling of many names, the elimination of some names from the roll,
and the addition of fifty-two members who had not been previously
reported. Therefore, it is apparent that the printed Roster of 1912
has many errors-some possibly the fault of the Grand Secretary's office, some of the printer, and some of the local Secretaries-and I
respectfully suggest that it would be useful to the craft of the Jurisdiction to publish one more Roster, with the names corrected to the
last reports.
I call your particular attention to the new aprons worn by the
brethren. · They were made by the girls at the San Gabriel Masonic
Home and compare well with the best product of Masonic supply
houses. Their efforts are commended to the Craft, and it is hoped
that Lodges of the Jurisdiction generally will remember them when in
need of linen aprons.
"'

At the risk of becoming tiresome, I renew my former suggestion
that life members be required to procure certificates of membership
annually.

87

"Resolved, that Section 129A of the Constitution be amended to
read as follows :
"Section 129A. No Lodge shall receive an application for the degrees of Masonry, or for affiliation, from any one who is engaged
either as principal, agent or employe in the saloon business ; and any
Mason who may hereafter enter upon and engage in the saloon business, either as owner, agent or employe, shall be deemed guilty of
unmasonic conduct, and shall upon due trial and conviction of said
offense, forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges, including membership in any Lodge, except when acting under order of any Court."
Since the last Annual Communication, six new Lodges have been
formed, the names and locations of which appear in the Address of the
Grand Master. The petitions for the dispensations for those Lodges,
together with that of Hammonton Lodge (dispensation for which was
continued last year), with the certificates of withdrawal of the several
petitioners from the Lodges whereof they had last been members, and
the certificates that the Masters and Wardens named, were duly qualified as required by the Constitution, were all correctly prepared, and
they are herewith submitted, together with the returned dispensations
and books of record and the petitions of the new Lodges to be perpetuated by charter.
Grafton Lodge No. 141, by error in its annual returns for the
year ending July 31, 1912, overpaid the Grand Lodge the sum of
$1.90, claim for which is herewith presented from said Lodge.
At the close of the last Annual Communication there were 351
chartered Lodges on the roll of the Grand Lodge, and one Lodge,
Hammonton, continued under dispensation. Three Lodges have with•
drawn from the jurisdiction, viz. ~ Manila No. 342, Cavite No. 350,
and Corregidor · No. 386, the said ·Lodges having joined in the formation · of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands. Six new Lodges
have been formed, at Maricopa, Claremont, San Francisco (Fairmount),
Los Angeles (Germania), Tyrian (Manteca), and Lancaster, makin~
the total number now on the roll, 355. The membership last year was
48,315. We lost by the withdrawal of Lodges in the Philippine Islands, ,
443 members. The membership. is now, as reported July 31, 1913,
50,257, a net gain of 1,942. There were initiated 3,198, passed 3,137,
raised 3,132, affiliated 977, restored 113, withdrawn 689, suspended for
non-payment of dues 491, suspended ~r expelled for unmasonic conduct
15, died 751.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Grand Lecturer read his annual report, which
was referred to a special committee consisting of George
F. Rodden, Charles F. Chapman, Rudolph Schaeffer, Walter S. Pierce, and William H. Nichols.
GRAND LECTURER'S REPORT.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit to you the report of my stewardship as Grand
Lecturer for the year just closed.
Masonry has kept well abreast of the times, carrying high its
torch of enlightenment, ever anxious and willing to impart light and
information to all those who desire to see the dawn of a new day.
The Brethren of this jurisdiction have much to be proud of, for
Masonry has never been in a more prosperous condition or the
Lodges more flourishing, numerically or financially.
All with very few exceptions have had more than the average
gain in membership. Six new Lodges have received dispensations
this year, and one held over from last year, making at present 355
Lodges. The net gain in membership being over two thousand and
the total membership being now over fifty thousand, what a vast
army when united for a principle and what a great influence when
exerted for the betterment of mankind!
The coming year promises to be one of unusual Masonic activity, largely because of the great number of people coming into
our State, and the wonderful improvement going on therein.
Masonry in California was never better organized than it is
today, and with a steady adherence to the fundamental principles
of the Fraternity and the splendid support of the many good and
true men who are giving their time and best efforts toward Masonic
uplift, satisfactory results will be attained.
In this forward movement each of us has a part. Let us then
all do our full duty as men and Masons, thereby making the coming
year one that will be resplendent with true fraternity and higher
manhood.
I have visited every district in the jurisdiction and held schools
of instruction, day and night sessions.
All have been well attended by officers and members with few
exceptions.
It is unfortunate that some of the Lodges located in the mining
districts, which in years gone by were flourishing Lodges when the

'1RAN:-> LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

99

mines were prosperous, now find it difficult to hold meetings on
account of not being able to get a quorum, the members being scattered all over the world.
I wish to thank the Inspectors for their assistance and courtesies
to me during the year. They have aided very materially in bringing the Lodges up to the present state of proficiency. I have received reports from all the Inspectors and they report the Lodges
in their respective districts to be doing good work and mcist of
them in fine financial condition.
Several of the Lodges have completed and dedicated new Temples
within the year and several are now working on plans and making
preparations to build in the near future.
Several degrees have been conferred by the Inspectors of this
City and the Bay Counties, in San Francisco and neighboring Cities,
and quite a number of degrees have been conferred by our Most
Worshipful Grand Master, who filled the East, and the Inspectors the
other places.
It has been my pleasure to accompany our Most Worshipful
Grand Master on many of his visits throughout the State, and on
several occasions the Third Degree was conferred by him letter perfect, which was not only instructive for the Brethren from a ritualistic
standpoint, but greatly appreciated by them.
It was also my pleasure to accompany the Most Worshipful
Grand Master on his visit to the Islands of Hawaii.
Schools of instruction were held by me both at Hilo and Honolulu, where I found the Lodges in excellent condition, and a more
hospitable, enthusiastic and earnest lot of Masons would be hard to
find. The splendid manner in which they have the work is remarkable in view of the fact that they had never before had· a· visit
or instruction from the Grand Lecturer.
This speaks well for our good Brother Inspector Tucker, who
attends the Grand Lodge regularly and carries home the ritualistic
work to those loyal Brethren of the Islands.
It certainly is a great source of gratification to be now installed
in our new home, our beautiful new Masonic Temple, which we have
all looked forward to with pleasant anticipation. The completion and
dedication of this imposing structure can not help but make us all
feel proud that we are Masons and members of this grand institution
whose motto is the Brotherhood of Man and the Fatherhood of God.
I desire to thank the V.". W.". Grand Secretary and his Assistant
for the many courtesies extended to me during the year.

The report is as follows:
REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF MASONIC HOMES.
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith submits, for your consideration and approval, its annual report for
the year ending September 30, 1913.
The M:. w:. Grand Master reappointed M:.- w:. Motley H.
Flint a Trustee, vice self, term expired, and the Board held its annual
meeting at the office of the · Grand Secretary, on October 26, 1912,
re-elected William S. Wells president, Motley H. Flint vice-president
and Elmer E. Stone secretary, and has, during the year, held regular
and special meetings, at both Decoto and San Gabriel.

lOll

The reports of the Secretary, Superintendent and Accountants are
herewith presented, made a part of this report and referred to for a
more particular statement of the financial and general condition of both
Homes.
At the request of the Grand Secretary and in o~der to conform to
his books, we have closed our financial stat~ment this year on July 31st,
and hereafter our financial year will correspond with that of the Grand
Secretary, and will run from August 1st to July 31st. Our general
report, however, will continue to be for the year ending September 30th.
We are pleased to report that, in our opinion, the water question
at Decoto has been solved and we have an ample supply. We continued our prospecting in which we were engaged and, as reported to the
Grand Lodge in our last report, by going down 250 feet in the fiat by
the barn without finding any large gravel strata, only two small beds
about one foot in thickness, which produced some little water, but not
sufficient. We then went to the fiat in the southeast~rly corner, near
the front line of our property on the County Road, and put down a
well, the log of which is as follows : Black adobe, 6 feet; clay and
rock, 12 feet ; yellow clay, 57 feet; water gravel, 1 foot;
yellow c.lay, 19 feet ; water gravel, 17 feet; yellow clay, 5
feet, makmg a total depth of 117 feet, which, upon test, developed 180
gallons a minute for seventy-two hours' run ; the water level, at the
commencement of the test, standing at 64 feet 6 inches from the surface and at the end 68 feet from the surface, which in a dry year, with
present conditions existing in the locality, would seem to assure us an
abundance. This well is twelve inches in diameter and has a double
casing with cement between for· the first forty feet, and we have been
pumping into the reservoirs since June 20th and all of them are full,
and kept full without any trouble, which means a total of 673,141 gallons OO' hand at all times, the capacity of the reservoirs being as follows:
Larize reservoir on the hill.............:._..........~- ............446,000 gallons
Small reservoir on the hill .......-·······-.:.·---........,..177,141 gallons
New concre~e tank or reservoir ................................ 50,000 gallons
Immediately upon being assured of ample water, we prepared plans
for a pipe line, pumping plant, boiler house, laundry and ice plant and
let contracts for same, and now have everything completed and ready
to operate.
We have built a concrete tank of 50,000 gallons' capacity, located
on the hill just below and easterly . of the main building, and we pump
from the well into this tank with electric power, using the water from
this for the entire fiat and all points below and the barns and chicken
yards. .We pt•mp from this reservoir · to the tWo reservoirs on the hill
with a steam pump, located in the heating plant.

The improvements are all permanent and first class in all respects,
and will, we feel, meet the approval of the fraternity.
The stone steps in front and on the sides of the main building
have been settling and cracking and, upon investigatic"on, we discovered
that they had no foundation, resting upon the adobe and not. going
down to bedrock. They have had to be torn out and rebuilt at quite
an expense.
Plans have been adopted and work on the new dormitory building
will soon be commenced, so that, by next year, we feel that we will
have accommodations for al! applicants.
The action of the Grand Lodge of last year, in providing for the
additional fifty cents per capita for building purposes, has enabled the
Board to provide and plan permanent improvements of a substantial
character that will be an ornament and a credit, and not temporary or
a makeshift, as in the past, and we feel that in a couple of years all
money necessary to put the institutions in first class condition will be
obtained and the tax can then be removed. A continuance, however, of
the same for a time will be the only way we can obtain sufficient funds
to continue our improvements and obtain the results contemplated.
The manner of handling our fuel oil at the railroad has been very
unsatisfactory, as we have no plant of our own and have to depend on
others, and, while it is quite an inconvenience at times, Mr. Salz has
taken care of it for us at his private plant as best ·he could. We
propose to remove the present oil tank to Decoto and put up a complete plant of our own to take care of our fuel oil, which will give
us a storage capacity of 15,000 gallons at the depot, in addition to our
storage at the Home. This will necessitate a pump and an electric
motor and a building of some kind to house it.
Immediately upon finding water, we bad same analyzed and found
it to be a first class water for drinking purposes. Upon the completion
of the well, we had another analysis made, with the same result. After
filling the reservoirs and pumping out of the well for some three
months, and finding the water somewhat troublesome in the boilers and
hot-water backs in the range, we had another analysis made, which was
practically the same and is as follows :

The following quotation from the report of the analytical chemists
will explain the conditions better :
"From the point of view of a potable water, this sample leaves but
little to be desired. The total salinity would generally be considered
high, but in this case the nature of the mineral ingredients-nearly 27
grains per gallon of carbonates-is such as to make the water more
palatable than otherwise, while contributing nothing of an unpleasant
or undesirable character.
"From the most important point of view-its freedom from deleterious organic matter-the water leaves nothing to be desired, and is
unhesitatingly recommended for drinking purposes.
"The chlorine content, interpreted as sodium chloride (common
salt), is generally, when as large as in this sample, associated either
with pollution from animal organic matter (in which event the 'free
ammonia' is invariably high), or occurs in waters found in close proximity to the sea. It is very probable that in the Masonic Home water
the chlorine is present, principally, as chlorides of calcium and magnesium, a fact which is, however, of no particular moment in the present
connection, and which there is not now time to determine, so that in
my report I have made the interpretation usual with chemists.
"Turning, now, to the use of the water where a sufficient temperature is applied, and we have quite another story, as your recent experience has shown, and as we saw when at the Home on Monday last.

The management at San Gabriel is good. All employees take a
deep interest in the institution and the children seem to inspire all connected with the Horne with a thorough spirit of working to their general
welfare. Much fruit and berries were put up this season and the gardens are in the best condition for years.
More interest in the Hornes is being manifested yearly and a larger
number of members of the fraternity are visiting and inspecting the
Hornes, many offering valuable suggestions and advice, an~ to these we
tender our sincere thanks, as well as to all who have contributed to our
Christmas fund and donated gifts.
The Superintendent and matrons have performed their duties with
zeal and fidelity and have materially aided us in the work.
we recommend that the usual per capita tax of one dollar be levied

"It is thus seen that in forming the deposit which has caused so
much annoyance the water simply follows natural laws which we cannot alter. But we can, by chemical means, cause the precipitation to
occur in a more convenient place and at a more convenient time, and
by sending a heated water ·of low carbonate content through the pipes
avoid the possibility of what would otherwise be a serious and· expensive
inconvenience.
"The means to which I refer is by the addition of lime to the water,
the operation being what is called a softening process, and effects the
removal of the so-called 'temporary hardness'-as that caused by calcium and magnesium carbonates is known, as distinguished from the
'permanent hardness' which results from the presence of sulphates."
From this it will be seen ,that some kind of a plant will have to be
provided for softening this water before it can be used in the boiler
and hot water system without danger of filling up the pipes and ca us-·
ing damage and expense.
The property at San Gabriel is in as good order as the age of the
improvements permits. The expense for repairs has been light, and no
new improvements have been found necessary or advisable. The resolution of the Grand Lodge of last year to erect fireproof buildings for
the children in the near future would make any extended improvement
ill-advised until definite plans of the.new improvement were determined,
that all improvements might be in harmony.
A local condition has arisen which gives the Board some little concern in regard to our schooling facilities and the expense of taxes on
the property. The town of San Gabriel recently incorporated and thelines of the city were so run as to take our institution within their city
limits. There are many unsatisfactory features in this arrangement.
Our building is a large one and it is the opinion of the Board that better
value can be realized by selling the building than by wrecking it when
the new buildings are contemplated. Our grounds are attractive and
we believe a sale could be made of our improved property for sufficient amount to purchase similar property near the present site and
supply half the fund for the new buildings. Besides the financial advantages, we would be relieved of the possible annoyance of unnecessary
regulation by ordinances of an incorporated city. We recommend,
therefore, if deemed expedient by your Trustees-, that they be author-
