SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.
Decoto, Alameda County, Cal., October 1, 1913
To the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes of California:

Gentlemen : The undersigned presents the fifteenth annual re
port as Superintendent of the Masonic Homes of California.
The past year at the Decoto . and San Gabriel H?mes has been
a most prosperous one. The new permanent buildings, improvements and repairs made will enable the Homes to give a higher
standard of service in the care of the older and younger wards of
the fraternity. A good family spirit prevails and every effort is
being made by the management to realize by conscientious and patient
work, the cherished ideals of our fraternal Homes.
To the older ~embers, wqo, enfeebled by advancing years, are
unable to leave their Home for social recreation, entertainments and
diversions of various kinds are provided, to brighten the daily routine
of their lives.
To the younger members, both in their home and school life,
every influence possible is brought to bear, to prepare them for
future careers of usefulness. All the members of our large family
are encouraged to render some service in keeping with their strength,
for the upbuilding of the Homes and in their leisure hours, to interest themselves in healthful and wholesome enjoyments, in and
out-of-doors, for their physical, mental and moral well-being.
DECOTO.
Since last report 24 persons have been admitted to the Decoto
Home; 19 have passed away and there have been 2 departures.
There are now present at the Home 75 men and 39 women. Every
room is occupied and as admissions can only be made as vacancies
occur, the need for additional room is most urgent to meet the
demands of the Lodges throughout the jurisdiction.
The health of the Home has been good, with the exception of
those who by reason of age, are becoming infirm and helpless.
The openi~g of the Coleman Hospital, thoroughly equipped with
all the advanced medical and sanitary devices, enables our physician
and trained nurses to give to those who are ill, the very ·best medical
attention. There are now twelve members of the family being cared
for at the hospital.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

113

The new refrigerating plant enables the Home to properly care
for a large supply of meat, milk, butter, eggs and vegetables, and
manufacture at the same time all the ice for our needs.
The new steam plant supplies all the steam heat and hot water
for present demands and is large ...nough to care for the requirements of the future. It also· furnishes power for the pumping of
water to the large reservoirs and for the operation of the new
laundry.
The new laundry is equipped with the latest improved Troy
laundry machinery and can handle all . the needs of the Home for
many years to come. The laundry work has been done by contract
and has not been satisfactory. The operation of our own plant will
turn out better work at a far less cost.
The recent development of water on the flat, an inexhaustible
supply, has solved for all time the water problem. The newly built
reservoir situated south of the main building, furnishes water for
irrigation, and the water in the old reservoirs can be piped to any
part of the home property, making possible the planting of trees,
lawns, flower and vegetable gardens, alfalfa fields, and affords plenty
of water for fire protection. Owing to the dry season and the continued shortage of water from the springs, the returns from the farm
have not been good this year, and the walks, roads, lawns and gardens have received but little attention.
The greater portion of the hill part of the ranch has been leased,
either on shares or cash rental The hay crop was somewhat short
and the quantity raised was not equal to last year's crop. A brooder
house and several chicken houses have been added to ' the chicken
ranch. An incubator has been purchased and a large number of
chickens, ducks and turkeys have been hatched and raised. The
chicken and hog ranch and dairy have also been improved and given
good returns. The vegetable gardens have been enlarged and sup~
plies a variety of fresh vegetables for the table and plenty of greens
for the farmyard.
·
The orchards produced a fair crop of fruit, all over and above
the needs of the Home was sold in the San Francisco market. The
berry garden has furnished a good supply of berries for table use
and preserves. A large quantity of fruit has been preserved for
winter use by the ladies of the Home, and much of the mending
and making of household linen has · also been done by them. A.
number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare of the ·
Home by their labors in the carpenter, tailor, shoe· and barber
shops, and in light work in a general way.
·
All the mattresses and pillows throughout the Home have been
made over and encased in new ticking.

A fully equipped barber shop has been presented to the Home
by the Lodges of the 39th District. At their expense, a room in
the Annex building has been plastered, tinted and the wainscoting
has been white enameled, electric fixtures installed the floor covered
with linoleum. The shop has been fitted out wlth a wa~h stand,
hot and cold water faucets, hydraulic barber chair, buffet stand, cup
and brush case, two large mirrors, chairs, shaving and hair cutting
tools, towels, etc. It has supplied a great need at the Home, for which
the brethren are very grateful.
The library has been enlarged and 300 books, wnich have been
donated, have been placed on the shelves". The reading rooms have
been well supplied with magazines and daily papers.
Each Saturday afternoon throughout the year, a moving picture and musical entertainment has been given at the Temple. The
usual services on Sunday have also been held. A Home reading
club has been organized, regular meetings are held in the Assembly
hall. This gathering is specially for the benefit of those, who by
reason of failing sight, are unable to read. The subjects for reading are carefully selected. All of these meetings are well attended.
Many entertainments have been given for the pleasure and benefit
of the family by Lodges, members of Lodges and their ladies. All ·
holidays have been observed in the usual way. The following is a
list of those who have contributed to our enjoyment: Members of
Sequoia Lodge No. 349, with their ladies; the Country Club of Washington Township;. Nobles of Islam Temple, A. A. 0. N. M. S., with
their ladies; concert by the Islam Shrine Band; Oakland Lodge No.
188, with their ladies; Hon. J. R. Knowland, Panama lecture illustrated with stereopticon views ; Brooklyn Lodge No. 225 ; Eucalyptus Lodge No. 243; Sequoia Lodge No. 349, each conferred a
third degree at the Temple. A musical concert by the Pasmore Sisters. Most Worshipful Grand Master, William Parker Filmer as:.
sisted by Grand Lecturer, Thomas J. Baker, and the Inspecto~s of
the San Francisco Districts and .Bay Counties, exemplified the work
in the third degree at the Temple for the benefit of the brethren
of the Home. Also a number of small socials have been held among
the residents of the Home from time to time.

the splendid moral atmosphere created by. our most capable Matron,
and her able corps of assistants at the Home.
To the average visitor, the term "uneventful," as used above,
might seem a serious misnomer. The daily scene of from fifty to
sixty healthy, hearty, happy children, romping through their be>iu·
tiful grounds, singing at their work, ambitious and energetic in their
accomplishments taught them at the Home, striving for the perfect
in their music, their drills, and their school work, presents a continuous moving picture of the real joy of child life. The infrequency of disobedience of any kind, or even little quarrels among
themselves, or the display of selfishness in a child in sharing. his
playthings or provisions, is a condition rarely to be found in the
best governed families.
This year has experienced many changes in the personnel of
the children. The interest manifested by many of our well-to-do
Masons in providing places for our boys who become fourteen years
of age, is growing so that we have not boys enough to meet the
demand. The Board have determined their choices in placing the
boys, not by merit of the Mason making the request, but by selecting a position possessing conditions and environments, which in
their judgment were best suited to the temperament of the boy.
In this manner our boys are thrown in the hands of good men,
who are deeply interested in their present welfare and future success.
All of our boys who have left the Home in the care of Masons
are continuing their schooling, and advancing in their business
training, with one exception, and this boy, the Board feels, has had
his lesson and will not repeat his indiscretion. All the boys are
in touch at all times with some member of the Board and we are
in that manner able to keep in touch with their successes and ready
to assist in case any reverse or misfortune should be encountered.
While no general rule can be adopted for the care of our older
girls, and no general provision applicable to all can be made, it has
fortunately occurred with each girl as she approached the age that
she should · leave tlie home, that an opportune condition arose which
provided for her in the most suitable manner. There are now 35
boys and 24 gi~ls at the Home, making a total of 59 children.
·

SAN GABRIEL.
Our home for the children at San Gabriel has experienced an
active, pleasant and most successful ye3r, and yet we may say, almost uneventful as far as concerns anything unusual in their home
life. The prevailing good discipline, and the thoroughness of our
11ystem, of which we are particularly proud, gives little opportunity
for either accidents or the advent of outside influences to destroy

they were used at the Home. Ordinarily, there would be great
responsibility attached to moving such a number of children, either
to the beach or to the mountains, where they are exposed to so
many chances of accident and danger, but our children are so dependable we feel no concern at all in the undertaking.
The general improvement in the accomplishments of the children
is most encouraging. The boys are clever and accurate in their
work, quick in perception and intelligent in execution. Their cadet
drill rivals m ny Shrine Patrol companies and in all mechanical work
they display much skill. They are not lazy or procrastinating, and
cultivate a courteous and kindly behavior at all times.
The girls have advanced in music, sewing and art work, as well
as being proficient in all the essential duties of caring for a home.
The parlors, . reading rooms and other parts of the building give
constant evidence of their usefulness. Beautiful pieces of embroidery,
crochet work, pillow covers, tapestry, and attractive drawings display the industry of fifty or more busy little hands.
The Board desires to commend most heartily the work of our
piano instructor, Mrs. Lela Buckh<!,m, who practically donates her
services, and devotes so much time to the work. The children love
her and reward her with good results on the piano. We will lose
Miss Olcott this year, as she has accepted a position in a school
in Cleveland. She leaves the Mandolin Club, however, in splendid
position to continue their work themselves for awhile.
Visitations at the Home by members of the Grand Lodge and
of the various lodges of California are fruitful of good results. The
children are taught that they are indebted to the Masons of California for their care, and they are pleased when those taking an
interest in them caU at their Home. Most Worshipful William P.
Filmer, our Grand Master, has called almost every time he came
to Los Angeles. The children feel they know him and his .cordial
handshake and cheerful manner will never be forgotten. Brother
Baker, our Grand Lecturer, enjoys a big place in their hearts, and
his visits are anticipated with much pleasure. Past Grand Master
Brother WeUer, and Brother Whicher, have also won strong favor
with them by their continued interest and visits with them.
A notable visit each year is. that of the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles. The first Sunday of May the Board holds its
meeting in the parlors of the Home, and after Sunday School the
children provide a program for the Board whicl} invariably inspires
interest with the Lodges constituting this Boar<l. This also gives the
officers of the Lodges of Los Angeles an opportunity to see the
children at home, visit all portions of the building and grounds, and

become more intimately acquainted with this feature of the work of
our great Order.

The donations to the children this year were liberal, and particularly appropriate to the occasion or season when given. Many,
many minor donations and timely' treats or kindnesses were shown,
that space would not permit recording here, but they gladdened many
little hearts at the time, and the donors were liberally compensated
by the evident gratitude of the children.
Dr. J. M. Dunsmoor, Past Master of Hollenbeck Lodge, Secretary of the Board of Relief, and active in all lines of work, still
cares for our children in case of illness, and is our constant adviser
in all matters of prevention and cure. He is devoted to the children
and refuses compensation for his work. The Board desires the Grand
Lodge to know how greatly we are indebted to him for his most
necessary and most valuable services.
Closely associated with Dr. Dunsmoor is Mrs. Ola Taylor, who
always attends him in case of an operation for adenoids or enlarged
tonsils or similar troubles; and whose sweet influence and bright
presence mean much to our big family.
Alhambra Lodge, Brother J. N. Hall, its Master, and the ladies
of the Eas"tern Star in Alhambra, are always contributing to the
welfare and comfort of the children.
Brother Alex Culver of Southern California Lodge No. 278
has contributed kindnesses too numerous to mention.
Al Malaikah Shrine are always thoughtful of the children, and
after each banquet the children are given a liberal supply of provisi;ns, and when the character of their entertainment permits, the
children are invited to enjoy it or participate in it.

Most Worshipful Grand Master William Parker Filmer and
members of the ·Grand Lodge have made a number of visits to the
Homes, also many of the brethren and friends interested in our
welfare have spent pleasant hours with us.
I wish to extend to the Matrons my appreciation of the loyal
assistance rendered and the conscientious and painstaking efforts
given to the work in their respective departments.
The Homes are entering a new era of development. The growth
during the past year has enlarged its field of usefulness. To care
for · and bring peace into the lives of those who have passed the
days of Autumn, to guide and train our little ones in the Springtime of their lives, requires a continuation of kind, practical methods
to meet the problems of the coming year, and calls for a renewed
consecration of spirit, crowned with deeds of service.
Respectfully submitted,

Dl!AR SIRS AND BRO'l'Hl!RS :
The Masonic Board of Relief, of the °City of Los Angeles, herewith presents the following report of its labors from September 1,
1912, to August 31, 1913.
The Masonic Board of Relief is composed of the Masters (ex
officio) of the 22 Blue Lodges of this City and two members appointed by ·him, together with the Past Grand Masters residing
within the City of Los Angeles, the Inspectors of the several Masonic
Districts of Los Angeles City, the Manager of the Masonic Employment Bureau, and one Past Worthy Matron of the Order of
the Eastern Star.

140

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

· PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Stated Meetings are held on the first Sunday of each month.
The Officers form an Executive Board and are on duty daily.
The year 1912-13 has been one of great prosperity in Masonic
Circles, as well as in other walks of life. Yet with all this prosperity there has been the proportional amount of suffering and distress.
California, and particularly Southern California, is known to
have the most genial climate extant, and Los Angeles being the
most prosperous and rapidly growing city on the Pacific Coast, has
brought hordes of mechanics, laborers and professional men and
women to our midst.
Yet as prosperous as we are, there is such a thing as having
too many people for the positions which we have to offer. Our
Masonic brethren must compete with the profane in the battle of
life, and unless they have sufficient means to maintain themselves
and their families, until they can secure positions they must be
aided. 'l'his has been the experience of far too many applicants
for relief.
Again, too many in~alids are sent to Southern California, in
the vain hope that they can secure employment, while our balmy
atmosphere and invigorating sunshine restore them to health. And
while in some instances their hopes are realized, yet in a majority
of cases they have put off their coming till it is too late. These
people must be provided for here or returned to their homes to
pass quietly away among their friends.
Brethren, the glorious climate of California is not the fountain
of perpetual youth, neither is it the cure-all for every infirmity.
We try to do our duty as Masons to those who have a right
to our consideration, as we see it, but please bear in mind that
"To err is human; and to forgive is Divine."

RECORD OF

VISIT TO THE MASONIC HOME.

On May 4, 1913, the Board of Relief accepted the invitation
of Brother E. B. Spencer, the Trustee having especial charge of
the Masonic Orphans' Home at San Gabriel, and held its session
in the spacious parlOr of that institution.
·This was followed by a delightful entertainment by the children of the Home consisting of drills, marches, recitations, vocal
and instrumental music, after which the building and premises ~ere
carefully inspected, and finally returning to the city by special car.
To several members, this visit was a revelation. Brethren, visit
your Masonic Home. Learn what Masonry is doing, and will do
for you should necessity require.

Chairman; C. E. Powell, Treasurer; J. ]. Warner, Secretary.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

bearing date June 3, 1863. The history of Masonry in South Dakota,
and the history of the State itself, are practically contemporaneous, and
the observation is made that St. John_'s Lodge has not only given inany
distinguished Masons to the jurisdiction but also eminent statesmen to
the commonwealth.
'
·
Under Necrology, he refers to the death within the year of that
well-beloved friend and c~mpanion, Most Worshipfui Oscar S~ Gifford,
Past Grand Master, one who was closely identifie.d with the progress
of Dakota for over forty years, and who was held in hfgh. esteem by
thousands of friends eve~ywhere. He was a ~ell-kno~n figure for
many years in the Grand Lodge of South Dakota, and his genial presence and kindly coun~el, we are assured, will be ·greatly missed.
Seven Lodges which recei.ved charters at the preceding Annual
Communication were duly constituted, and t.he account of the 300-mile
auto trip of Grand Master McMakin, through Indian reservation and
scenic lands to 'constitute certain of these Lodges, is v.ividly set forth
by the Grand Master, with accompanying pictorial illustration, in his
strong address.

From the report of the Grand Secretary, information is obtained
that the members in good standing at this time exceed a total of
10,000, a gain of 522 being recorded for the year.

TEXAS.

1912.

In compliance with the prov1s1ons of the Constitution of the
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Texas, Ancient Free and Accepted
Masons, the Seventy-seventh Grand Annual Communication was held
at the Masonic Temple, in the city of Waco, commencing on Tuesday,
the 3rd day of December, A. D. 1912, A. L. 5912, at 10 :00 o'clock a. m.,
Sam P . Cochran, Grand Master, in the Chair.
The first subject to which the mind of t he Grand Master reverts,
after the Grand Lodge is assembled, is the loss w11ich the Grand Lodge
has suffered in the year in the passing onward to his place in the
Supreme Grand Lodge above of the Most Worshipful Dr. Thomas M.
Matthews, the Senior Past Grand Master of Masons of Texas, who
was called to his reward on June 14, 1912, he having attained t he
ripe age of eighty-two.
Notwithstanding Dr._ Matthews' advanced age, his intellect remained
strong and virile to the very last. For many years he conducted the
Department of Foreign Correspondence in the jurisdiction of Texas,
and he was known throughout the Masonic World as a valued contributor for many years to Masonic literature. His various reports as
Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence give him front
rank among Masonic writers. His command of English was, it has
been stated, wonderful, his diction was pure and bis understanding of
Masonic lore and literature was so complete that his expositions of

..
REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

law were illuminating and forceful: The vast fund of information
contained in the numberless pages written by· him during the years
of his long life will prove of priceless value to his brethren. "The
Brethren of Texas," says the Grand Master in his eulogy, "are proud
of the ·career of this good man and Mason and will ever hold in
grateful remembrance his noble and distinguished service in behalf
of Ancient Craft Masonry, cherishing the hope that the lofty sentiments, high ideals and courtesy as seen in his life and labor, will •be
a help and inspiration to men and Masons everywhere."
To give an idea of the vast extent of the jurisdiction of Texas, it
may be stated that twenty-three Lodges that received charters at the
preceding Annual Communication were constituted during the year,
either by the Grand Master personally, or by his duly authorized
deputies, and eight dispensations were issued to form new Lodges,
and as further evidence of the extent of the operations of this Grand
Lodge, it may be mentioned that corner··Stones to twenty-nine public
buildings, school houses, Masonic buildings, churches, etc., were laid
during the year under Masonic auspices.
.
Permission was refused by the Grand Master in at least one case
to a Lodge to attend in a body Divlne Service. We think the Grand
Master's judgment in refusing permission in this case is sound. We
believe it is not· in accordance with our understanding of Masonry
that Blue Lodges should attend seNices of denominational churches.
Individual Masons should, by all means, perform the duty of ;i.ttending
upon frequent occasion divine services. in such churches as suit their
individual views and predilections, but it is, in our judgment, distinctly inappropriate for a Masonic Lodge in regalia to attend ·some
denominational church. Ancient Craft Masonry is founded upon the
belief in the Fatherhood of God and Brotherhood of Man, and is
supposed to be sufficiently broad and comprehensive to gather within
its encircling arms those who can unite upon these two grand propositions, but when it comes to singling out some particular denominational
church to ·assemble in in Masonic regalia, we think it is distinctly
inappropriate, notwithstanding the fact that a number of jurisdictions
on this contine.nt, particularly the Canadian Jurisdictions, favor the
idea, and frequent permissions are given by Grand Masters to attend
divine service in regalia.
A number of decisions were rendered by the Grand Master constructive of the local law and constitution of Texas, none of the decisio'ns, in our opinion, being of sufficient general importance to quote.
A number of rulings upon "physical disqualification" were made by
the Grand Master, and Texas is one of the jurisdictions that still holds
to the theory that a man must not only be possessed of inward qualifications, but of outward perfection as well before he can be made a
Mason.

While the benefits of Masonry in its operative days were quite
properly limited to those possessing physical strength, there is now in
speculative Masonry, which is the. only Masonry with which we deal,
or of which we have any knowledge, no reason for demanding such
absolute physical soundness such as is required by certain of our
American Jurisdictions, and which would exclude an applicant such as
was done a few years ago in this jurisdiction, because he was shy a
lobe of his left ear, or because, as in another case, a toe nail was
missing.
"It is the inner and not the outer qualifications," as we are taught
in the first degree, "that recommend· a man to be made a Mason,"
and, in our opinion, we should look more for soundness of character
r.ather .than absolute perfection of limb, in selecting our material for
Masonry'; and, furthermore, in our judgment, the position of the
Grand Lodge of England upon this subject contains a very large
degree of soundness in that it remands the decision in these cases to
the subordinate Lodges.
Consideration is given quite extensively by the Grand Master to
the s1,1bject of clandestine Masonry. This subject has caused this
Grand Jurisdiction, as it has caused other Grand Jurisdictions in recent
years, no little trouble; but a recent decision by the Supreme .Court
of Louisiana where suit was brought against the Grand Lodge by a
certain individual who claimed the right to establish so-called Cerne.a u
Scottish Rite Masonry iri Louisiana, on the ground that the Grand
Lodge, through its Grand Master, or some other official, had branded
this particular form of alleged Masonry as clandestine; and asking
damages therefor, decided that the established and universally recognized Grand Lodge of Masons was the recognized and supreme
authority on the subject within the jurisdiction, and had the right to
brand as clandestine and put upon it the brand of outlawry any interloping bodies calling themselves Masonic, and that the recognized
Grand Lodge bad absolute authority and could drive these pretenders
out of the State.
·
Under that decision there ought to be no trouble in regular Grand
Lodges ridding the various jurisdictions of these grafting fakers,
whose only purpose in sailing under the name "Masonic" is to rope
in the unwary and get their money by pretending .to sell them Masonic
degrees. They are frauds in all cases, and it is right and proper that
the courts of law should protect' the people against impostors of this
character.
In conclusion the Grand Master assures his brethren that the
remembrance of the year of service which he has given to the cause of
Freemasonry in Texas as Grand Master, will be one of the fondest
recollections of his life, and furthermore that the welfare and wellbeing of the grand organization will ever be his fondest hope.

The report of the Grand Secretary discloses the fact that there
are now in Texas more than 56,<XX> Masons, and that a gain of nearly
2,200 over the preceding year was made.
Texas certainly is one of the finest Masonic jurisdictions in the
world, and that is in particular one feature of Texas Masonry that
lifts it to a very high plane, reference being made to the Masonic
Orphans' Home.
There are now at the Home under the guiding and directing care
of matron and superintendent and teachers, who are vitally interested
in their welfare, 206 orphan children. A school is maintained at the
Home (the children are not sent to the public schools) where a full
corps of competent, thoroughly equipped teachers impart instruction
and conduct a school much superior to the average public sc)10ol of the
State. A kindergarten is provided for the little ones, and for the more
advanced, literature, domestic science, stenography, bookkeeping, typewriting, mechanical and electrical training, military tactics, drill, etc.,
and at the same time their moral and religious training is not neglected.
Some American Jurisdictions where the Ma.sonic Home idea has
been decried, and where so-called Educational Funds have been laud~d
as supplying the same service as that'performed by the Masonic Home,
have reported, as can be easily pointed out from their reports, that
during a year few, if any, applications have been made to those having
these Funds in charge for disbursement for the benefit of orphans.
It is not possible to conclude from the fact that no applications have
been made that no cases exist demanding this relief. The trouble is
they do not reach the cases and a complete answer is made to arguments of this character (where systems of this kind are put forth as
a proper substitute for the Masonic Home) by pointing to such jurisdictions as Texas where they have over 200 orphan children in their
Home, training them to become useful men and women, thereby supplying a leaven to raise the standard of citizenship of the entire commonwealth.
The Home in Texas has only been in existence something like
thirteen years, and we find that it is now not only the object of the
greatest pride to the jurisdiction but is regarded by the people at
large as one of the valued institutions of the State.
The report of the President and Trustees of the Masonic Home
contains a statement of general interest, which we quote as follows :

doing a wonderful amount of good in maintaining Homes for

Homes in successful operation in the United States, and eight
other Grand Jurisdictions are accumulating a fund for the same
purpose. These Homes provide accommodation for over 3,000
beneficiaries, and during their existence have sheltered and cared

VERMONT.

1913.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of Vermont convened in its rooms in the Masonic Temple,
city of Burlington, on Wednesday, the 11th day of June, A. L., 5913,
at the hour of 10 o'clock in the forenoon, Eugene S. Weston, Grand
Master, presiding.
In opening his Annual Address, the Grand Master makes clear
his belief in the Masonic teaching that one should never enter upon
any great and important undertaking without first invoking the blessing of the Deity, and in this connection indicates his conviction that it
is only because Freemasonry has ever acknowledged divine guidance
that it has• survived the vicissitudes of the ages.
In welcoming the Grand Lodge, and in looking over the assemblage,
representative of a membership of nearly 14,000, his mind goes back
in retrospect to the assembly of those who gathered 120 years before
to form the Grand Lodge of Vermont.
The original meeting comprised fourteen brave and valiant .soul.s,
'strong in their belief in Freemasonry, strong in patriotic impulses ahd
love of country, men who had endured hardships and privations as
pioneers in a new country; three of them, so the Grand Master s~ates, •
were with Ethan Allen when he marched upon the fortress of Ticonderoga, and others of the fourteen served their country in the War
for Independence.
The Grand Master gives expression to the thought that the
Masons in Vermont may well be proud that they can trace their
Masonic ancestry to men cast in such heroic molds as these.
In speaking of Fraternal Dead, the Grand Master especially refers
to Herbert L. Townsend, Grand Tyler, who passed away early in the
current year; also Brother Henry L. Stillson, for many years a member of the Committee on Credentials in the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master paid personal visits within the year to all but
two of the districts and from these personal visitations, and otherwise,
he is able 'to report that the Craft is in a healthy condition in all
respects.
·
The Grand Lodge was convened in August, 1912, to dedicate to
Freemasonry, Virtue and Universal Benevolence, the hall of Mt. St.
Anthony Lodge No. 13; and on October 23rd a Special Communication
of the Grand Lodge was held for the purpose of laying the cornerstone of the New Haven High School Building.
A little friction between the Grand Lodge of Vermont and the
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts over a matter of dual membership,
involving the right of a member of the Vermont Lodge to hold, without

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

15j.

demitting therefrom and while still a member of the Vermont Lodge,
membership in a Massachusetts Lodge. Correspondence between the
two Grand Jurisdictions was characterized by the utmost courtesy,
and the matter which threatened misunderstanding was finally adjusted
to the complete satisfaction of the Grand Master of Vermont, the
Grand Master of Massachusetts disclaiming any purpose to offend the
Jurisdiction of Vermont, although under the law of Massachusetts dual
membership is permitted, something very rare in American Grand
J arisdictions, although usually recognized as permi~sible by the Grand
Lodge of England.
The Grand Master refers to his visit to Alexandria, Virginia, upon
the occasion of the meeting of the George Washington Masonic Memorial Association on February 21st and 22nd. Very little appears to
have been accomplished at this meeting beyond the mere exchange of
social and fraternal courtesies.
The Grand Master speaks of the subscriptions made up to thfs
time, amounting to about $2,000, $500 of the amount )laving been used
for expenses, leaving a balance of about $1,500 still in the hands of the
local committee. The Grand Master states in his report of this meeting that he supposed that the subscription of Vermont for membership
in the association was to go to the building fund, but he finds that it
was used to promote the enterprise.
The Grand Master expresses a little doubt as to the practical value
10 the outside jurisdictions of a Memorial Hall at Alexandria, Va.,
and makes a statement, in which a great many will concur, that, viewed
from the standpoint of sentiment, he fails to see wherein outside jurisdictions are called upon to assist the local Lodge at Alexandria, Va.,
over which Washington once presided, in erecting such a building as
is projected, and about the only value he can see to the participating
Grand Lodges is that this building will make a yearly meeting place
for the representative Masons from the several jurisdictions, and will
give a chance for the interchange of ideas that may possibly benefit
those who participate.
We fail to agree that it has value for this purpose, and we believe
that a so-called "clearing house" for Grand Lodges in settling matters
of dispute is not a proper or necessary adjt1 nct of ancient Craft
Masonry in America.
A small number of so-called decisions are quoted by the Grand
Master, none, however, of general interest. The Grand Master is constrained to the belief . that possibly the Grand Lodge of Vermont is
11ot manifesting to any marked degree its function• of Masonic
diarity.
The question of Masonic charity has, so he states, been up for the
attention of the Grand Lodge many· years. The Grand Master states

158

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

that he himself, wherever occasion has offered, for twenty years pa~t
advocated some action on the part of the Vermont Grand Lodge,
looking to the establishment of something permanent in the nature of
a Masonic charity.
He calls attention to the large number of jurisdictions in the United
States supporting Masonic Homes, and in su,ch jurisdictions as have
no Homes a large number are accumulating funds, the incomes of
which are' intended for the relief of the aged and infirm. or the
orphans. He calls attention to the State of Delaware, with only
twenty-two Lodges and a membership of a little more than 3,000,
having within the year dedicated the Masonic Home.
He calls attention to Maine, with a membership about as large as
Vermont, with a fund of $60,000 for charitable purposes; to New
Hampshire with a similar membership and a fewer number of Lodges
maintaining a Masonic Home; to Idaho with only thirty-one Lodges
and a membership of 3,568, with a Fund known as the Orphans' Fund;
and he contrasts these jurisdictions with Vermont, with neither a Home
nor a Fund.
.
The Grand Master urges that something definite in the direction

The One Hundred and Thirty-fifth Grand Annual Communication

T he Grand Master, in the Introduction of his Address to the
Grand Lodge, extends . felicitations to the brethren upon the marked
prosperity which the jurisdiction is enjoying, and gives expression to
the sentiment t~at_ as the members of the Grand Lodge gather in
Annual Communication from year to year, they should pledge themselves to a renewal each year of service to their brethren, in exemplifying in their lives the fundamental doctrines of the Fraternity-the
Brotherhood of Man resting upon the Fatherhood of God.
Joy, he states, quickly turns to sorro'IY in the ·realization brought
home to them that the death angel may at any moment touch some
loved one, and this thought is deeply impressed at this moment upon
the Grand Master, for he states that his ·report was written, and the
dosing words had been added, when the news was flashed over the
wires bringing sorrow to thousands of Masonic hearts in the announcement that the Grand Secretary, Right Worshipful George W. Carrington, had, almost without warning, been called to "come up higher."
Brother Carrington was one 'of the best known Masons of the
jurisdiction and his unexpected demise came as a shock to his brethren.
Another beloved brother of this jurisdiction was called to his
rewa rd within the year, Brother John Moncure, affectionately known
as the "Bishop of the Poor."

.
One of the questions propoundetl, and the answer given, was as
follows:
The by-laws of a certain Lodge provided that the stated meeting
shall be at 8 :00 o'clock. The Master, through error, opened at 7 :30'
o'clock, the ballot was spread, and petitioners elected and subsequently
received all the degrees.
Does the error of the Master impair the regularity of the election
of the candidates, no objection being made until they had received
all degrees?
The Grand Master's answer is as follows:
"The Master erred in opening his Lodge contrary to the by-laws.
but his error does not affect the Masonic status of those who were thell'.
elected and subsequently received the degrees."
The decision is unquestionably sound, although some, devoted to
technicalities; would maintain that if the Worshipful Master could
open the Lodge thirty minutes in advance of the time provided for in
the by-laws, and the meeting be considered legal, he could, on the
same principle, open the Lodge an hour, or twenty-four hours, b~fore.
the time stipulated in the by-laws and the meeting and the business
transacted therein would, for like reasons, be legal.
The fact, however, that the slight variation in the hour of the
meeting described in the query was not for the p_urpose of ~'snap.
judgment" or other ulterior purpose, but that an innocent mistake·
had been made, and furthermore that there was no objection ta~en at
the time and that the degrees were subsequently conferred without
objection, certainly justified the Grand Master in declaring that . the

,

161

Masonic status of those who received the degrees was not adversely
affected through error.

adopted:
"From the earliest history of this Grand Lodge it has claimed
the right to jud~e of the fitness of material residmg in this Grand
Jurisdiction. While recognizing the right of another Grand Jurisdiction to exercise perpetual jurisdiction over rejected material
while residence continues in that jurisdiction, we still affirm our
right as a Sovereign Grand Lodge to accept material, otherwise
qualified, regardless of previous rejection in another Grand Jurisdiction."
This unquestionably is the sensible doctrine, and coincides with
California's position on this question.

WISCONSIN.

1913.

The Sixty-ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Wisconsin was opened in
Ample Form in the Masonic Building, corner of Jefferson and Oneida
streets, in the city of Milwaukee, at the hour of 2 o'clock p. m.,· on
Tuesday, June 10, 1913, A. L. 5913, Grand Master David B. Greene
in the chair.
,
The Grand Master, in his annual address, refers to the representative character of the gathering which he is addressing, being composed of men manifesting an unusual order of intelligence, influence
and ability.
·
He calls their attention to the fact that they are assembled on no
pleasure excursion nor idle junket, ' but to do the great work of
Masonry in its efforts to upbuild and bring to a degree of perfection
human society, of which the Grand Body of Masonry forms a part.
He comments upon the wonderful age in which we live, an age
of progress and science ; an age in 'Xhich the mere credentials of popularity and antiquity are not sufficient to secure standing and recognition, but an age that demands to know what is going forward now;
an age that scrutinizes politics, social customs, even religious ideas,
and because of these facts the Grand Master points out that the
Masonry of today, if it is to receive approval, must justify its existence
by pointing to current deeds and achievements.
He makes it clear that, in his judgment, no institution is better or
stronger than are the members who compose it, and hence, if Masonry
is to do good and be an instrument of usefulness in the world the
members that compose it must exemplify Masonic precepts.
'
It has often been affirmed, says he, that Masonry is entitled to a
position among the human institutions, simply because of its charity,
and if it were not for its system of benevolence the institution would
be as hollow as "sounding brass."
The Grand Master concedes the vital character of charity in connection with Masonry, but contends that Masonry has stood in all
times past, and stands today, for other principles of priceless ~alue to
humanity than those related to charity.
.
Masonry stands, he affirms, for the absolute equality of men, and
1t stands today for the intrinsic rights of the individual against the
encroachments of wealth or position; that it stands for the freedom of
thought, for the purity of the home, for the brotherhood of the
man, etc.
It is true that theoretically Masonry does stand for the absolute
equality of men. In other words, that all men in Masonry "meet upon

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

the level," and that individual merit and worth are the true titles to
distinction, and that, in accordance with this doctrine, Masonic preferment and honor are open to all alike.
So far as American Mason.ry is concerned, we believe this is true,
and that neither wealth nor influence of any kind has material weight
in the question of honor or preferment in Masonry. This, however,
can scarcely be statetl of Masonry in other lands; and the Mother
Grand Lodge of England, which by many is considered the only true
source of legitimate Masonry, accords its highest positions of honor
and distinction to the members of the nobility only.
The position of Grand Master of Masons of England is always
filled by a Prince of the Royal Blood, and, regardless of what the theory
may be, any but princes are absolutely excluded . from the position of
Grand Master. This is true in England, and it is almost universally
true in all of the Grand Lodges in the political dependencies of Great
Britain. It is "Lord Carmichael,'' or "Lord Chalmsford," or "Lord
Plunkett," or "Lord Bishop of Perth," etc., who have, one may almost
say, always been Grand Masters of the Grand Lodges located in the
political dependencies of Great Britain, and these Lords are re-elect ed
year after year as Grand· Masters of their jurisdictions, and almost invariably they are political efficers of the Crown, usually the GovernorsGeneral of the provinces or countries to which they are sent from
England; and it would indeed be a manifestation of monumental assurance for any ordinary member of any of these Grand Lodges tu aspire
to the exalted position of Ruler of the Craft; hence when we say that
merit is the only recommendation to preferment, and that all Masons
stand upon the level, we should make at least some mental reservations.
The Grand Master adverts to a fact which, we believe, is generally true, that the bulk of the correspondence passing between Grand
Jurisdictions is in reference to matters touching the conferring of degrees, out of courtesy or by request.
If it were the custom to grant <limits to Entered Apprentices or
Fellowcrafts, as is the custom in most foreign jurisdictions, this mass
of correspondence between subordinate Lodges of different jurisdictfons in America, through their respective Grand Masters, would be
avoided.
The Grand Master refers to the invitation received by him from
the Grand Master of Indiana, asking him to attend a conference of
Grand Masters, to be held in the city of Indianapolis in March, 1913;
but because the purpose of the conference was not definitely stated, the
whole affair being nebulous and uncertain, so far as its purposes were
concerned, the Grand Master declined, very sensibly, in our OP.inion,
to accept the invitation.

reviewed.
He refers to Brother Monroe's address as business like and voices
his approval of certain of the Grand Master's recommendations.
GEORGE B. WHEEU:R, elected Grand Master, Eau Claire.
WILLIAM W. P:ERRY, re-elected Grand Secretary, Milwaukee.

The Grand Master reports that the Masonic Order in Wyoming is
makini a strong and healthy growth. Four dispensations were issued
by him for the formation of new Lodges "in towns," as he states,
"whose present condition and future prospects insure permanency,
etc."
He reports the financial condition of the jurisdiction as "distinctly good."

170

WYOMING.

1912.
The Thirty-eighth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Wyoming, Ancient Free and Accepted Masons, was held in Cheyenne,
Wyoqiing, September 4th and 5th 1 Grand Master Harold Banner presiding.

171

Concerning the Masonic Home project, which is under consideration in this jurisdiction, and for the creation of which a fund has been
in process of accumulation for several years past, the Grand Master
says:
"I am convinced that the time is coming, and will soon be here,
when many of our brethren in Wyoming will need our care and
attention for the brief span of life that lies before them, and to the
honor of Freemasonry and of common humanity I am thankful
to know that we are year by year increasing the fund that will
enable us to build and maintain a home wherein these deserving
old men may pass their declining years in self-respect and peace."
Among the decisions rendered by the Grand Master, we find the
following:
"Question-Can a man who is blind in one eye petition a Masonic
Lodge for membership?
"Answer-Yes. If his sight is good he is not physically disqualified."
We commend this decision to the consideration of Pennsylvania
and South Carolina and Texas, and a few other jurisdictions, where
the loss of even an eyelash would almost disqualify.
Four Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held for the
purpose of laying corner-stones of public buildings, dedicating Masonic
Temples, etc.
The Grand Master gives a list of "official visitations," which is
evidence of his activity in promoting the welfare of the Craft during
the year.
For the first time in his many years of service as Grand Secretary,
the Very Worshipful W. L. Kuykendall calls attention to the "tabulated
statement of the membership," as evidence of the very healthful and
satisfactory growth of the fraternity.
He particularly directs attention to the fact that one of the Lodges
in the city of Cheyenne has a membership exceeding 300, and that the
city itself has 543 active members. The total increase in membership
during the preceding year was 206, "being about, if not the greatest, in
the history of the Grand Lodge."

172

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The following "liquor resolution" was adopted :
"Resolved, That no Lodge within the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of the State of Wyoming, A. F. and A. M., and holding its
charter therefrom, shall receive a petition for any degree from or
confer any degree upon any person engaged in the business of
selling intoxicating liquors as a beverage, and that her:eafter no
member of any Lodge aforesaid shall engage in said business under
the penalty of expulsion from said Lodge."
·.
This is in line with similar legislation in twenty-five or thirty of
our American jurisdictions.
The Report on Correspondence is, as usual, by the Grand Secretary,
Brother W. L. Kuykendall.
California, 1911, is briefly and courteously reviewed.
Brother Kuykendall in his "Conclusion" sets forth his views in a
convincing manner of the necessity of holding to sound and correct
standards in the "recognition" of Grand Lodges, and insisting, if the
current of Craft Masonry is to be preserved in its purity and saved
from hopeless pollution, recognition should be refused to Grand
Lodges spuriously tracing their Qrigin to certain irregular so-called
Scottish Rite Supreme Councils, and otherwise.
He takes a strong and logical position against the right, which has
apparently been conceded by two or three American Grand Jurisdictions, of "individual recognition." That is, the right of a Mason belonging to one jurisdiction to recognize and treat as a Mason one
belonging to another jurisdiction, which latter jurisdiction has not
been recognized as regular, and entitled to recognition, by the Grand
Lodge of the jurisdiction to which the first Mason belongs, thereby
?i:-tually conceding to the individual Mason the right to exercise a
~ r lCtion belonging, legitimately and properly, to the Grand Lodge only.
Wu.LIAM PUGH, Grand Master, Evanston.
W. L. KuYXJ!NDALL, Grand Secretary, Saratoga.
Respectfully submitted,
:itpt. 8, 1913.

EDWARD H. HART,
Chairman of the Committee.
